# PREFACE

THIS new text of the Ethiopic Version <note>The Ge'ez language version of the Book of Enoch, which preserved the most complete text of the work through the centuries.</note> has been the labour of many years. It is practically exhaustive; for no pains have been spared to secure a first-hand and complete knowledge of the MSS. <note>Abbreviation for manuscripts.</note> evidence. I have not, however, restricted myself to the mere task of publishing the Ethiopic Version as it is found in the best MSS.; for this Version, even when first made, exhibited many unintelligible passages, which were due either to the mistakes of the Ethiopic translator, or to the corruptions of the Greek text before him, or to the mistakes of the Greek translator, or ultimately to corruptions of the Hebrew text before the Greek translator. With these various sources of corruption I have sought to deal: in some cases, I think, with indubitable success: in others, my reconstructions are at the best merely provisional and tentative. In this work Halévy <note>Joseph Halévy (1827–1917), an Orientalist and traveler who argued for the Hebrew origins of the text.</note> led the way and made a permanent contribution, but many of his reconstructions were valueless from the outset as they were based on Dillmann’s <note>August Dillmann (1823–1894), a pioneer in the study of Ethiopic texts.</note> inadequate text of 1853. As a result of these studies I have abandoned the view that Enoch was originally written in Hebrew, and come to the conclusion that, like Daniel, it was written partly in Aramaic and partly in Hebrew.

The Greek and Latin fragments have been printed in parallel columns with the Ethiopic Version and their relations with it have been fully discussed in the Introduction.

The Ethiopic text has been printed directly from a photograph of the chief MS. *g* <note>A specific manuscript designation used by scholars to identify a particular source document.</note> with the necessary corrections from other MSS.; but the orthography <note>The conventional spelling system of a language.</note> of this MS. has been nearly always adhered to, although it very frequently confuses the aspirates and sibilants <note>Speech sounds produced with a breathy or hissing quality, which often became interchangeable in later Ge'ez writing.</note>.

<summary>The author introduces a comprehensive new edition of the Ethiopic Book of Enoch, detailing his efforts to correct textual corruptions and his conclusion that the original work was composed in both Aramaic and Hebrew.</summary>
<keywords>Ethiopic Version, manuscripts, Joseph Halévy, August Dillmann, Book of Enoch, Book of Daniel, Aramaic, Hebrew, textual criticism, orthography</keywords>

# PREFACE

In a work of this nature, where sometimes in a single page there are 800 acts of collation <note>The process of comparing different manuscripts to identify variations in the text.</note> and verification, mistakes are inevitable, and, where such do occur, I can only ask for the kind indulgence of the student.

My best thanks are due to the late Mme. d’Abbadie for permission to collate four manuscripts and photograph two others that were at Abbadia; to the librarian of the British Museum for permission to photograph its ten manuscripts of Enoch; to the librarians of the Paris and Munich Libraries for the courtesy with which they lent the Ethiopic <note>The classical language of Ethiopia, also known as Ge'ez, in which the most complete version of Enoch survives.</note> manuscripts in their charge to the Bodleian Library for my use; to the librarian of the Berlin Library for the loan of its splendid manuscript together with permission to photograph it; to the librarian of the Vatican for permission to photograph its manuscript of Enoch; to Baron von Westenholtz of Hamburg and Mr. Garrett of Philadelphia for having lent for my private use their manuscripts of Enoch through the kind offices of Dr. Enno Littmann; to my niece Madeleine La Vie Charles for much help in making the *Index of Greek Words* <note>original: "Index Graecitatis"</note>; to Mr. A. E. Cowley for revising the reconstructions of the Semitic original in the first thirty chapters; and, lastly, to the Trustees of the Revised Version Surplus Fund for a grant <term>subvention: a formal financial grant or subsidy</term> towards the expenses incurred in my expedition to Abbadia at the foot of the Pyrenees.

Finally, I cannot conclude without expressing my deep gratitude to the officials, and especially to the readers and compositors, of the Press for their skilled services in the publication of this text.

->R. H. CHARLES.<-

# INTRODUCTION

### § 1. THE BOOK OF ENOCH—ITS FORTUNES. ORIGINALLY WRITTEN IN PROSE AND VERSE, AND PARTLY IN ARAMAIC AND PARTLY IN HEBREW.

IT is seldom that authors attain to the immortality which they hope for, and it is still more seldom that anonymous authors achieve this distinction. And yet it is just such a distinction that the authors of the Book of Enoch have achieved. That such should be ultimately his lot was the deep-rooted conviction of one of this literary circle. He looked forward (chapter 104, verses 11, 12) to the time when his writings would be translated into various languages, and become to the righteous ‘a cause of joy and uprightness and much wisdom.’ This hope was in a large degree realized in the centuries immediately preceding and following the Christian era, when the currency of these <term>apocalyptic<note>A genre of ancient religious writing focused on revealing heavenly secrets or the end of the world.</note></term> works was very widespread on account of their distinctively religious and predictive contents. But from the fourth century of our era onward they fell into discredit, and under the ban of such authorities as Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a prominent bishop and theologian.</note>, Jerome <note>The scholar responsible for the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible translation.</note>, and Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo, one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> they gradually passed out of circulation and became lost to the knowledge of Western Christendom till about a century ago. It was not, however, till recent years that the Book of Enoch and similar works have begun to come into their own, not indeed on the ground of their intrinsic religious worth, but from their immeasurable value as being practically the only historical memorials of the religious development of Judaism during the two centuries which preceded the birth of Christianity, and particularly of the development of that side of Judaism to which historically Christendom in large measure owes its existence.

In the course of editing the present work it suddenly dawned upon the editor that much of the text was originally written in verse. This discovery has frequently proved helpful in the criticism of difficult passages.

Another conclusion, to the adoption of which a prolonged study of the text has led the editor, is that the Book of Enoch like the Book of Daniel was originally written in two languages—in Hebrew and Aramaic.

<summary>This introduction outlines the historical disappearance and modern rediscovery of the Book of Enoch, highlighting its importance for understanding the Jewish roots of Christianity and its original poetic and bilingual composition.</summary>
<keywords>Book of Enoch, Church Fathers, Jewish history, Aramaic, Hebrew, apocalyptic literature, biblical criticism</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly introduction to the Book of Enoch, focusing on the linguistic origins of the text and its subsequent translations into other ancient languages.</meta>

<page-num>x</page-num>
-># THE BOOK OF ENOCH<-

That the Book of Enoch was written in a Semitic language <note>The family of languages including Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, and Ethiopic.</note> is now accepted by everyone, but scholars are divided as to whether the Semitic language in question was Hebrew or Aramaic. Only one valuable contribution on this question has been made, and that by Halévy in the *Asiatic Journal* <note>original: "Journal Asiatique"</note>, April–May, 1867, pp. 352–395. This scholar is of the opinion that the entire work was written in Hebrew. Since this publication, however, fresh evidence bearing on the question has been discovered in the Greek fragment (chapters 1–32) found in Egypt. Since this fragment contains three Aramaic words transliterated <note>Written using the letters of a different alphabet to represent the sounds.</note> in the Greek, some scholars—and among them Schürer, Lévi, and N. Schmidt—have concluded that not only are chapters 1–36, but also the rest of the book, derived from an Aramaic original. 

In support of the latter statement no evidence has yet been offered by these or any other scholars, nor yet has there been any attempt to meet the positive arguments of Halévy for a Hebrew original of chapters 37–104, whose Hebrew reconstructions of the text have been and must be adopted in many cases by every editor and translator of the book. A prolonged study of the text, which has brought to light a multitude of fresh passages the majority of which can be explained by retranslation into Hebrew, has convinced the present editor that, whilst the evidence on the whole is in favor of an Aramaic original of chapters 6–36, it is just as conclusive on behalf of the Hebrew original of the greater part of the rest of the book. 

To determine the exact limits within which each language is used is a task of no little difficulty. This is due in part to the fact that for four-fifths of the text we have only a translation of a translation <note>Likely referring to the Ethiopic version, which was translated from a Greek version, which was itself translated from the Semitic original.</note>, and in part to the close affinities <note>Similarities and shared roots.</note> existing between Hebrew and Aramaic. For the resemblances between the two languages are so great, that frequently retranslation from the Ethiopic into either is sufficient to explain corruptions <note>Errors or changes introduced by scribes over centuries of copying.</note> in the former. Notwithstanding, there is a clear balance of evidence in favor of a Hebrew original of chapters 37–71 and 83–104. There is much room for further study of this question, and it is to be hoped that there will be fresh discoveries of manuscript evidence bearing upon it.

### § 2. GREEK, ETHIOPIC, AND LATIN VERSIONS.

The entire book was translated into Greek and from Greek into Ethiopic about the sixth century of our era, and possibly into Latin. These are fully dealt with in the following sections.

<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

### § 3. THE GREEK VERSION. EDITIONS OF THIS VERSION.

The Greek Version has only in part been preserved. Chapters 1–32:6 and 19:3–21:9 (the latter in a duplicate form) were discovered in 1886–1887 at Akhmîm <note>A city in Upper Egypt where a significant cache of Christian and apocryphal manuscripts was found in a monk's grave.</note> by the French Archaeological Mission at Cairo, and published by M. Bouriant in 1892. These are designated as Gᶢ and Gᶢ¹, and Gᶢ² in the case of the duplicate passage. Large fragments have been preserved in Syncellus <note>George Syncellus, a 9th-century Byzantine chronicler who quoted Enoch in his "Extract of Chronography."</note> 6–10:14, 15:8–16:1, and 8:4–9:4 in a duplicate form. These are designated as Gˢ and Gˢ¹, Gˢ² in the case of the duplicate passage.

The chief literature on these fragments is as follows:—

Bouriant, *Greek Fragments of the Book of Enoch*. *Memoirs published by the members of the French Archaeological Mission at Cairo*, volume 9, pages 91–136, 1892. This is praiseworthy as a first edition, but the text is disfigured by many errors.

— *The Gospel and the Apocalypse of Peter with the Greek text of the book of Enoch. Text published in facsimile by photogravure from the photographs of the Gizeh manuscript.* Paris, 1893.

Dillmann, *Reports of the Proceedings of the Royal Prussian Academy of Sciences at Berlin*, 1892, 51–53, pages 1039–1054, 1079–1092. These studies are of course good, and several of this scholar's suggestions are excellent. In his comparison of the Ethiopic and Greek Versions he had the benefit of having collations of *q t u* <note>Reference to specific Ethiopic manuscript codices used for comparison.</note> before him. These gave him no inconsiderable advantage in dealing with the problems before him, though his article takes cognizance of only a limited number of readings where these manuscripts furnish a superior text.

Lods, *The Book of Enoch, Greek Fragments discovered at Akhmîm, published with the variants of the Ethiopic text, translated and annotated.* Paris, 1892. Lods' contribution is learned, scholarly, and judicious, but as he had the misfortune to base his work on the corrupt text published by Dillmann in 1851, a large portion of his conclusions was vitiated <note>Spoiled or impaired in quality.</note> from the outset.

Charles, *The Book of Enoch*, pages 318–370. Oxford, 1893. In this work I attempted an exhaustive comparison of the Greek and Ethiopic texts, and carried the criticism of the materials several stages beyond previous scholars in this department. An overestimate, however, of the Ethiopic Version led me to make some unjustifiable changes in the Greek text. This error has been set right in the present edition. Notwithstanding, the subsequent thirteen years of study have confirmed most of the suggestions made in 1893.

<header>THE BOOK OF ENOCH</header>

Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek vol. III*. Students are very grateful to this scholar for the inclusion of the Enoch text in this edition, but the text as printed leaves much to be desired. It is occasionally unintelligible, where a comparison of the Ethiopic Version would have suggested the true text.

Radermacher, *The Book of Enoch, edited ... by J. Flemming and L. Radermacher*, pp. 18-60, 113-114. Leipzig, 1901. This text, on the whole, is well edited and forms an advance on preceding editions. But, unless I am greatly mistaken, Dr. Radermacher is not a Semitic scholar <note>A scholar of languages such as Hebrew, Aramaic, or Ethiopic.</note>. This deficiency in his equipment proved a sore handicap in the task he undertook. How is a purely classical scholar to edit a Greek text which is Greek in vocabulary, but largely Semitic in idiom <note>The "flavor" or grammatical structure of the language.</note>? To show that our text is of this character it will be sufficient to adduce the following passages: xxii. 9 "of which the spring of water is in it" <note>original Greek: οὗ ἡ πηγὴ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐν αὐτῷ</note> (Hebrew: *asher . . . bo* <note>אשׁר . . . בו</note>) = ‘in which there is the spring of water.’ xvii. 1 "in which those being there become" <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾧ οἱ ὄντες ἐκεῖ γίγνονται</note> (Hebrew: *asher . . . sham* <note>אשׁר . . . שׁם</note>) = ‘where the dwellers become.’ Here, it is true, "there" <note>original Greek: ἐκεῖ</note> could be taken with "those being" <note>original Greek: οἱ ὄντες</note>. xxxii. 3 "of which they eat of its holy fruit" <note>original Greek: οὗ ἐσθίουσιν ἁγίου τοῦ καρποῦ αὐτοῦ</note> (Hebrew: *asher . . . piryo* <note>אשׁר . . . פριו</note>) = ‘whose holy fruit they eat.’ The editor’s failure to recognize this idiom in xvi. 1, has led him to emend the text in such a way as to obliterate wholly its original form. The unemended text runs: "from the day . . . of death from whom the spirits going forth from the soul of their flesh."<sup>1</sup> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ ἡμέρας . . . θανάτου ἀφ᾽ ὧν τὰ πνεύματα ἐκπορευόμενα ἐκ τῆς ψυχῆς τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῶν.</note> This Semitic construction is supported by E <note>The Ethiopic Version.</note> though in a slightly corrupted form. Hence it must be preserved, though as I pointed out in 1893, there is according to E the loss of "the giants" <note>original Greek: τῶν γιγάντων</note> before "from whom" <note>original Greek: ἀφ᾽ ὧν</note>. This very phrase, moreover, "the giants" <note>original Greek: τῶν γιγάντων</note> is found in G<sup>s</sup> <note>The Syncellus Greek fragment.</note>, though this version inserts after it a gloss (?) containing the names of the three orders of giants as they are given in the Targum of Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> on Gen. vi. 1-4.

The text and notes are accurately edited, but there are some errors. In v. 6 Radermacher reads "the undefiled" <note>original Greek: οἱ ἀμίαντοι</note> as an emendation of the corrupt reading which he says is *ama | toi* <note>αμα | τοι</note> and not "sinners" <note>original Greek: αμαρτητοι</note>, as Bouriant and Lods stated. Bouriant and Lods were certainly wrong, and Dillmann’s edition and mine, which were necessarily based on the work of these scholars, shared in their error. The autotype reproduction <note>An early photographic printing process.</note> of the text was not published till after the issue of these editions. But if Bouriant and Lods deciphered the MS. wrongly, so also has Radermacher. It reads *amartoi* <note>αμαρτοι</note>. The *r* <note>ρ</note> is partially obliterated, but it is unmistakable in the photographic reproduc-

### § 4. THE RELATIONS OF THE Gˢ <note>The Syncellus fragment</note> AND Gᵍ <note>The Gizeh fragment</note> TO EACH OTHER AND TO E (THE ETHIOPIC VERSION).

(a) *Gˢ more original than Gᵍ.* These two fragments are closely related and yet exhibit marks of independence. They are closely related, and probably go back to the same Greek translation of the Aramaic text, since they present in so many passages identically the same text. On the other hand Gˢ has in several passages a different and undoubtedly better order of text. Thus Gˢ rightly places vii. 3–5 of Gᵍ (or rather its equivalent of vii. 3–5) after viii. 3 of Gˢ. For manifestly vii. 1, 2, viii. 1–3 precede vii. 3–5. Thus it alone preserves the original order. The angels went in to the daughters of men, who bare to them three classes of giants. And the angels taught their women sorceries and incantations (vii. 1, 2). Then follows a detailed account of the art, which each of the leading twenty angels taught mankind. And after this the giants turned against men and began to devour their flesh (Gˢ viii. 1–3; Gᵍ viii. 1–3, vii. 3–5). It will be observed that in viii. 3 Gˢ is very defective compared with

Gˢ <note>The Greek version preserved by the Byzantine chronicler George Syncellus</note> in the list of the offices of the various angels. The additional elements in Gˢ here could not have been written by a Greek, for in every instance the office constitutes when translated into Aramaic a play on the name of the angel who discharges the office. Similarly in vi. 7 the order of the names of the angels is different and Gˢ is here preferable to Gᵍ <note>The Greek version found at Gizeh (the Akhmim fragment)</note> E <note>The Ethiopic version</note>.

Again, viii. 4 of Gˢ has preserved in all probability a more original text than Gᵍ E. For it is natural that the substance of the prayer of men as they were slain by the giants should be given when it is first referred to in viii. 4. Here, indeed, Gˢ presents a duplicate text, and both texts give the prayer in question. Gᵍ E, on the other hand, do not give the words of the prayer till ix. 3, when the angels are presenting it before God. Gˢ in Semitic fashion gives the prayer *in full* <note>original: "in extenso"</note> here also.¹ Again the additional clauses ("go," etc. <note>original: "πορεύου κτλ."</note>) in Gˢ x. 2, 4 belong most probably to the original work but have been lost in Gᵍ E, see p. 24, note 25. The same is true of the addition in Gˢ ix. 9 with its peculiar diction, as is clear from a comparison of x. 9, 15.

Finally Gˢ preserves several right readings over against Gᵍ E. Thus "bind" <note>original: "δῆσον"</note> in x. 11 where Gᵍ E corruptly read "show" <note>original: "δήλωσον"</note>, "be condemned" <note>original: "κατακριθῇ"</note> in x. 14 where Gᵍ E read "be burned" <note>original: "κατακαυσθῇ"</note>. Compare also x. 7.

(b) *Relations of Gˢ and Gᵍ to E.* Even the most superficial study makes it clear that E and Gᵍ are more closely related than E and Gˢ or Gˢ and Gᵍ. Indeed the evidence makes it clear that *E was translated from a manuscript which was also the parent or ancestor of Gᵍ*. This follows from the fact that *the same corruptions appear in Gᵍ E over against true readings in Gˢ where this exists*. Thus they both give impossible readings in x. 7 †"they smote" <note>original: "ἐπάταξαν"; Gˢ reads "they said" (εἶπον)</note>; x. 11 "show" <note>original: "δήλωσον"; Gˢ reads "bind" (δῆσον)</note>; x. 14 †"be burned" <note>original: "κατακαυσθῇ"; Gˢ reads "be condemned" (κατακριθῇ)</note>; xiv. 8 †"they were troubled" <note>original: "ἐθορύβαζον"; a mistranslation of the Aramaic original</note>, †"they spread out" <note>original: "ἐξεπέτασαν"</note>; xiv. 18 †"mountain" <note>original: "ορος"; corrupt for "vision" (ὅρασις)?</note>; xv. 9 †"of the higher ones" <note>original: "ἀνωτέρων"; Gˢ reads "of men" (ἀνθρώπων)</note>; xviii. 5 †"carrying in a cloud" <note>original: "βαστάζοντας ἐν νεφελῇ"</note>; xxii. 4 †"they made" <note>original: "ἐποίησαν"</note> for "they were made" <note>original: "ἐποιήθησαν"</note>; xxv. 5 †"into life" <note>original: "εἰς ζωήν"</note>; xxviii. 2 †"from the seeds" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν σπερμάτων"</note>. In ix. 6 all the authorities are corrupt, but Gᵍ E agree closely.

Furthermore, they add xv. 10 against Gˢ as well as the sense of the passage, and omit the same clause in x. 2, 4 against Gˢ. To the above facts we should add that E agrees with Gˢ in transposing vii. 3-5 from

On the other hand, the Ethiopic version <note>original: "E"</note> *preserves certain original readings lost by the Greek Gizeh manuscript and vice versa*. Thus the Ethiopic and the Greek Syncellus fragment <note>original: "G^s"</note> rightly add "to them" <note>original: "αὐτοῖς"</note> after "they were born" <note>original: "ἐγεννήθησαν"</note> in chapter 6, verse 1 and read "King of those who rule as kings" <note>original: "βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων"</note> in chapter 9, verse 4 where the Greek Gizeh manuscript reads "King of the ages" <note>original: "β. τῶν αἰώνων"</note>, and "authority over all" <note>original: "πάντων τὴν ἐξουσίαν"</note> in chapter 9, verse 5 where the Greek Gizeh manuscript reads "all the authority" <note>original: "πᾶσαν τ. ἐξουσίαν"</note>, and attest "among the females" <note>original: "ἐν ταῖς θηλείαις"</note> in chapter 9, verse 8 and "against one another from themselves against themselves" <note>original: "εἰς ἀλλήλους ἐξ αὐτῶν εἰς αὐτούς"</note> in chapter 10, verse 9, which the Greek Gizeh manuscript in both cases omits. Moreover, in chapter 9, verse 11 the corruption in the Ethiopic = "the things against them" <note>original: "τὰ εἰς αὐτούς"</note> (for "permit them" <note>original: "ἐᾷς αὐτούς"</note> so the Greek Syncellus) is easy of correction, whereas the Greek Gizeh manuscript offers the hopeless "aias" <note>original: "αιας"</note>. In the following passages the Greek Gizeh manuscript *omits clauses and passages preserved by the Ethiopic*. Thus it omits by homoeoteleuton <term>homoeoteleuton: a scribal error where the eye skips from one word to a similar ending later in the text</term> clauses in 9:1, 5; 10:16; 12:3; 14:3; 15:2; 18:3, 5, 11, and without any such intelligible ground 2:3, all of chapters 3 and 4 except six words, words and clauses in 6:1, 5; 9:8; 10:10, 19, 20; 14:14; 15:4, 8; 16:1; 19:1; 22:5, 8; 24:1, 2; 27:1. On the other hand, the Ethiopic *omits words and clauses preserved by the Greek Gizeh manuscript in 1:1, 9; 5:1, 3; 10:1, 2; 13:7; 14:25; 15:11; 20:8; 22:2, 5; 26:1.*

Naturally the Greek Gizeh manuscript and the Ethiopic have severally developed corruptions which it is generally possible to emend in either case by the help of the other. Thus the Ethiopic reads in 1:9 "they were firm" <note>original: "ረሰዱ፡"</note> for "they found" <note>original: "ረከቡ፡"</note>; 2:1 "they observed" <note>original: "ጠየቁ፡"</note> for "observe ye!" <note>original: "ጠይቁ፡"</note>; 9:4 "because" <note>original: "እሰመ፡"</note> for "Thou" <note>original: "አንተ፡"</note>; 12:1 and 2, 18:9 "morning" <note>original: "ጽባሕ፡"</note> for "fire" <note>original: "እሳተ፡"</note>. See also notes on 14:2, 21, 24, 25; 18:7, 9, 13, 16; 19:2; 20:2, 6; 21:7, 9; 22:1, 2, 3, 5, 8; 23:4; 24:3, 5; 26:3, 4; 27:5; 30:1; 31:2, 3; 32:2. In the following passages the Ethiopic presupposes "together with" <note>original: "ὁμοῦ μετά"</note> for "they shall be like" <note>original: "ὁμοῦνται"</note> in 5:6; "the things after these" <note>original: "τὰ μετὰ αὐτά"</note> for "metals" <note>original: "μέταλλα"</note> in 8:1; "I bring up" <note>original: "ἀνάγω"</note> for "I might read" <note>original: "ἀναγνῶ"</note> in 13:4; "of mystery" <note>original: "μυστηρίου"</note> for "of ten thousand" <note>original: "μυρίων"</note> in 18:16; "as peaceful ones" <note>original: "ὡς εἰρηναῖαι"</note> for "into sirens" <note>original: "εἰς σειρῆናς"</note> in 19:2; "to the people" <note>original: "λάῳ"</note> for "to the chaos" <note>original: "χάῳ"</note> in 20:5; "hollow" <note>original: "κοῖλοι"</note> for "beautiful" <note>original: "καλοί"</note> in 22:2, 3. ### § 5. THE LATIN VERSION AND QUOTATIONS.

The Latin Fragment, which constitutes a very imperfect reproduction of chapter 106, verses 1–18, was discovered in 1893 in the British Museum by Dr. James, the present Provost of King's College, Cambridge, and most kindly placed at my service for publication in my edition of *Enoch* in 1893. In the same year he issued it in the Cambridge Texts and Studies II, No. 3, *Apocrypha Anecdota* <note>original: "Apocrypha Anecdota", meaning "Unpublished Secret Writings"</note>, pp. 146–150. According to Dr. James this fragment is found in an eighth century manuscript (MS. 5, E xiii in Casley's *Catalogue of the Royal MSS.* now in the British Museum). In this manuscript the Enoch fragment is preceded by a penitential edict of Saint Boniface, and followed by an anonymous tract '<term>Concerning the Punishment of Sinners</term>' <note>original Latin: "De Vindictis Peccatorum"</note>. ²

The text has suffered from additions, omissions, and corruptions, and is very seldom a literal rendering of the original for many words together. Notwithstanding, it makes some contribution to the formation of a better text of chapter 106.

This manuscript further may point to a Latin translation, or at least to a partially completed Latin translation of Enoch; for (1) occurring in the midst of original Latin treatises it appears to have been found in Latin by the collector or scribe of these treatises. (2) It has suffered much

See chapter 5, verse 9; chapter 10, verse 7 (note 6); chapter 9, verse 4 (note 20); chapter 14, verse 8 (see p. xxix); chapter 17, verse 7 (note 14: see also pp. xxix–xxx); chapter 46, verses 4, 6 (note 35); chapter 52, verse 9 (see p. xxxi); chapter 99, verse 6 (see p. xxxiii).

## § 6. THE ETHIOPIC VERSION AND MANUSCRIPTS.

The Ethiopic Version has been preserved in twenty-nine manuscripts <note>abbreviated as MSS.</note> of which fifteen are to be found in England, eight in France, four in Germany, one in Italy, and one in America. Of these manuscripts there are only three of which my knowledge is indirect and slight, but not yet too slight to enable me to estimate their value and their relationships <note>original: "affinities"</note> with the other manuscripts. These manuscripts are *p* and *z, z₁*. Of these *z* indeed was most kindly lent to the Bodleian Library for my use, but unhappily I was absent part of the time of its stay there, and whilst I was present the officials of the Bodleian did not notify me of its arrival. *z₁* is of no account as it is merely an exact transcript of *b*. Next as regards *p*, this manuscript formerly belonged to Lord Crawford and was lent by him to the editor of the German edition of the Ethiopic text of Enoch which appeared in 1901, but since that date this manuscript has passed into the hands of a lady, who refuses to lend it or any other manuscript in her possession to the Bodleian Library for the use of English editors. Of the remaining manuscripts I have directly examined twenty-two, that is: *g, g₁ m q t u, a b f h i k l n o*, and *s u v w y a₁ b₁*. Of these I photographed thirteen, that is: *g, g₁ m q t u, f h i k l n o*. Five others, that is: *a b y a₁ b₁*, I had no need to photograph, as

The above division is indeed found in one manuscript, i. e. *h*, but this manuscript was unknown to Dillmann when he made his text. Moreover, the chapters in *h* vary frequently in length from those in Dillmann's text.

### § 7. RELATIONS OF THE ETHIOPIC MANUSCRIPTS.

(a) *Two forms of text, α <note>Alpha</note>, β <note>Beta</note>, of which β is late and secondary.* There are two forms of the Ethiopic text. The first is represented by *g g₁ m q t u* (and in some degree by *n*), which we shall henceforth designate by *α*, and the second, which owes its origin to the labors of native scholars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, by all the remaining manuscripts, i. e. *β*. The result of these labors has been on the whole disastrous; for these scholars had neither the knowledge of the subject-matter nor yet critical materials to guide them as to the form of the text. Hence in nearly every instance where they have departed from the original unrevised text they have done so to the detriment of the book. But it is not to be inferred from the above that *α* always represents one type of text and *β* another

This statement holds true in a much greater degree of *α* <note>The alpha group represents the older family of manuscripts.</note>. Indeed, the cases are comparatively few where *α* differs as a whole from *β* <note>The beta group represents a later, more "corrected" or standardized family of manuscripts.</note>. Moreover, when the attestation of *α* is divided, the individual or group of *α* attesting the right reading will often have the support of *β* or of groups within *β*. The above facts serve to prove that the recension <note>A systematic revision of a religious or literary text.</note> was not the work of a few years, but was rather a process which culminated in such a text as we find in *β*, but particularly in the MS. *v*.

(*b*) ***β* or groups in *β* sometimes preserve the original texts.** Again it is noteworthy that in a limited number of cases *β* preserves the original text where *α* is secondary. Some of these are no doubt accidental, but seventeen$^1$ such readings in thirty-two chapters are hard to account for in this fashion. These instances are found in the following passages. Thus *β* is right over against *α* in vi. 6 (note 43), viii. 3 (note 18), ix. 1 (note 6), 3 (note 18), *β*-*l* in ix. 1 (note 7), x. 1 (note 24), *b c e f h l$^2$ n o* against *α* and rest of *β* in vi. 6 (note 4), *abx* in ix. 4 (note 24), *bcox a p b* in xviii. 4 (note 12), *dy* in xxii. 13 (note 53), *h o p* in xxiv. 3 (note 47), *n a* in ix. 6 (note 10), *ox p* in xviii. 15 (note 32), *n* single-handed in ix. 11 (note 15), x. 3 (note 37), 7 (note 21), xxii. 9 (note 29). Hence in some cases there is in *β* most probably a survival of the original text where it has been lost in the present representatives of *α*.

(*c*) **The character and affinities of the chief MSS. *g*.** Of the MSS. of *α*, *g* is decidedly the best all-round MS. This does not mean that it has more unique and right readings than any other MS. of the older type of text, but that when all the good points of the various MSS. are summed up, *g* comes out an easy first. In the first thirty-two chapters *g* alone attests the right reading in vi. 5 (note 37), xvii. 3 (note 27), xviii. 7 (note 33), xxi. 5 (note 8), xxviii. 3 (note 11). In lxxxix. 42 (note 4) it has only the support of *n*, the best of the second class MSS. This MS.

Notwithstanding, it is by far the best representative we have of the ancient text. *m*. This manuscript is in some respects the weakest of the older group. It attaches itself so closely to *g* that we must assume it has come under its influence. This fact becomes of importance when we come to chapters 97:6b–108:10, where we have both *g* and <sub>1</sub>*g*.

Moreover, the evidence is not as decisive as we could wish; for though alone or together with β it agrees in many passages with *g* (see 97:6 (note 28); 98:2 (note 19) (along with β), 3 (note 29); 102:1 (note 1), 6 (note 2); 103:2 (note 2), 13 (note 15); 106:10 (note 6)), yet we find it displaying similar affinities with <sub>1</sub>*g* (see 98:6 (notes 13, 15); 99:2 (note 2); 103:2 (note 51), 6 (note 34), 7 (note 41); 104:1 (note 5); 105:2 (note 32); 106:7 (note 24), 10 (note 1), 19 (note 34)). On the other hand, in the vast majority of its unique readings, <sub>1</sub>*g* is unaccompanied by *m*. Hence, somehow *m* has been influenced by the readings of both *g* and <sub>1</sub>*g*. In 10:2 (note 33) and 17:4 (note 36) it alone preserves <note>attests</note> the original <note>primitive</note> text; in 7:3 (note 9) alone with *f*, and in 15:11 (note 21) with *b x y*.

*q*. Though teeming with every form of error common to the transmission of a text—such as additions, corruptions, and omissions—this manuscript contains a larger number of unique original readings than any other used in our text. Thus, it alone preserves the original text in 9:8 (note 21), 10:11 (note 16), 14:1 (note 39), 21:2 (note 24), 22:9 (note 25), 24:2 (note 41), 26:3 (note 33), 27:4 (note 47), 32:4 (note 31). It is more closely related to *g, <sub>1</sub>g,* and *m* than to *t* and *u*.

Notwithstanding, as *u* is a valuable <term>MS.</term> I have most faithfully recorded all its omissions and changes. *n*. Of <term>MSS.</term> of the second class *n* is by far the best. Thus it stands alone in giving the original text in chapter 9, verse 11 (note 15), chapter 10, verse 3 (note 37), verse 7 (note 21), and chapter 22, verse 9 (note 29) (?). Alone of <term>MSS.</term> of the second class it gives along with various <term>MSS.</term> of the first class the true text as in chapter 1, verse 3 (note 18), chapter 14, verse 21 (note 10), chapter 25, verse 7 (note 19), chapter 89, verse 42 (note 4), etc. Thus *n* exhibits the characteristics of both types of text.

With *a* in a less degree *k* is connected. *eh* and *op*, moreover, have also a considerable number of readings in common, and likewise *dloy*.

A study of the notes will show the reader that it is possible to establish partial connections between other groups of <term>MSS.</term> than those already mentioned, but the further prosecution of this subject does not lead to any valuable results.

# § 8. EDITIONS OF THE ETHIOPIC VERSION.

Laurence, *The Ethiopic Version of the Book of Enoch*. <note>original: "Libri Enoch Versio Aethiopica"</note> Oxford, 1838. This text was issued simply as a transcript of *a*, one of the manuscripts <note>abbreviated as MSS.</note> brought to Europe by Bruce, the great Abyssinian traveller, in 1773. The transcription is not very accurate in the early chapters, though the errors are as a rule easy to correct. In chapters 5–10 there are ten; most of these have passed over into Dillmann’s *Critical Apparatus* <note>term: Apparatus Criticus; the list of textual variations found in different manuscripts</note>, and from Dillmann’s to Flemming’s. As the text advances it becomes more accurate, so that I found its citation by Dillmann to be sufficiently trustworthy for use in the present edition.

Dillmann, *The Book of Enoch, in Ethiopic, edited according to the faith of five manuscripts, with various readings*. <note>original: "Liber Henoch, Aethiopice, ad quinque codicum fidem editus, cum variis lectionibus"</note> Leipzig, 1851. This edition was based on five manuscripts *a b c d e*, of which *a b* are in the Bodleian <note>The main research library of the University of Oxford</note>, *c* in the Frankfort Library, and *d e* were the property of the well-known traveller, Robert Curzon. Of Dillmann’s collations <note>term: collation; the process of comparing different manuscripts to identify differences</note> of *b c d e* I have tested only that of *b* in the opening chapters, and found only one bad error, in chapter 7. These five manuscripts are all of secondary value. The best of them is *a*. No further work on the Ethiopic text appeared till 1892, when Dillmann (*Reports of the Proceedings of the Royal Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin*, <note>original: "Sitzungsberichte d. kgl. Preuss. Akad. d. Wiss. zu Berlin"</note> 1892, 51–53, pp. 1039-1054, 1079-1092) published some variants from three manuscripts on the first thirty-two chapters of Enoch in connection with his edition of the fragmentary Greek Version.

Charles, *The Book of Enoch translated from Professor Dillmann’s Ethiopic Text emended and revised in accordance with hitherto uncollated manuscripts and with the Gizeh and other Greek and Latin Fragments*. Oxford, 1893. This translation was based on a drastic revision of Dillmann’s text. Ten new manuscripts, which belong to the British Museum, were used, three of them, *g, g*¹ *m*, being of primary importance, and seven, *f h i k l n o*, being of only secondary. Of these manuscripts I collated *m, f h i k l n o* on about three hundred passages; but *g, g*¹ I collated throughout, on the whole accurately, but defectively, as I now find, in a relatively small number of passages.

Flemming, *The Book of Enoch: Ethiopic Text edited by Joh. Flemming* (= *Texts and Investigations*, <note>original: "Texte und Untersuchungen"</note> New Series, VII. i). Leipzig, 1902. Dr. Flemming’s text is based on fifteen manuscripts, *a b c d e g, g*¹ *m p q t u v w y*. Of these six belong to the first class *g, g*¹ *m q t u* and the

<page-num>xxvi</page-num>
->THE BOOK OF ENOCH<-

rest to the second class. This editor has been at no little pains in the preparation of his text. Thus he has himself collated <note>Collation is the process of comparing different manuscript copies of the same text to identify variations.</note> *g m p q y*. His knowledge of *t u* he owes to photographs taken by Professor Meyer in France, and of *v w* to collations of the same scholar. It was a fatal error on Dr. Flemming's part that he did not photograph *g m q*, or, at all events, revise his collations of them.

Flemming's text naturally constitutes an immeasurable advance on that of Dillmann <note>August Dillmann (1823–1894), a pioneering German scholar of Ethiopic studies.</note>, and a considerable advance on Dillmann's text as emended in my commentary in 1893. With the help of the three new first-class MSS. <note>MSS. is the standard abbreviation for manuscripts.</note> *q t u*, this editor was able to point out a few passages where I followed mere idiosyncrasies of *g*, and also some others where I preferred the less trustworthy of the two texts *g, g* in chapters xcvii. 6^b—cviii. 10.

On the whole, Flemming's text is good, as might be expected from so excellent an Ethiopic scholar, and several of his suggestions have been accepted in the present edition. On close examination, however, Flemming's edition proves unsatisfactory from its frequent inaccuracy in the collation of the MSS. generally, and its inadequate collation of the first-class MSS. In my review of this edition in the *American Journal of Theology*, pp. 689-703, 1903, I have summed up its serious shortcomings under the following heads: (i) *Inaccurate and defective collation of the MSS.*; (ii) *The adoption of inferior readings into the text where the MSS. evidence for the true text is incontrovertible.* Flemming's treatment of the great Berlin MS. *q* on chapters x-xxxii will exemplify his method in dealing with the other MSS. In six passages in these chapters *q* alone amongst the Ethiopic MSS. preserves the true text of E <note>E refers to the Ethiopic version of the text.</note>, as is proved by G <note>G refers to the Greek version of the text.</note>. Yet in two of them, xxi. 2 (note 24), xxiv. 2 (note 41), *q* is not collated at all, and in the remaining four, x. 11 (note 16), xiv. 1 (note 39), xxii. 9 (note 25), xxxii. 4 (note 31), the reading of *q* is relegated to the notes, and the wrong reading adopted. In x. 7 (note 21) *q* practically gives the original text (which is preserved by *n* alone), but the corrupt text is adopted by this editor. (iii) *Corrupt passages are left in the text without any attempt to emend them or even to call attention to their viciousness.* (iv) *Divergencies between G and E are left unexplained.* (v) *Practically no use is made of the Semitic background for purposes of emendation.* <note>Emendation is the process of correcting a text where it appears to have been corrupted by scribal errors.</note> Notwithstanding the above shortcomings, Dr. Flemming's edition is deserving of the gratitude of Orientalists <note>A historical term for scholars of Near Eastern, Middle Eastern, or East Asian languages and cultures.</note>, as it constitutes a vast advance on that of Dillmann, and forms on the whole a serviceable work for students generally.

# INTRODUCTION
xxvii

### § 9. ORIGINAL LANGUAGE OF CHAPTERS VI—XXXVI—ARAMAIC; OF I—V, XXXVII—CIV—HEBREW.

That the Book of Enoch was originally written in a Semitic language <note>A family of languages including Hebrew, Aramaic, and Arabic.</note> is now universally admitted. But what that language is is still a question of dispute. In the past Hoffmann, Jellinek, Dillmann (?) assumed a Hebrew original, and Halévy (*Journal Asiatique*, 1867, pp. 352–395) furnished excellent grounds for such a belief, but of late years, since the discovery of the Gizeh Greek fragment, there has been a tendency to assume that the original was written in Aramaic. Neither view can I believe be established, but each appears to be true in part, as I hope now to prove. The proof in certain sections amounts almost to demonstration: in the case of others only a probability can be indicated. The results of present study of this problem tend to show that chapters vi–xxxvi were originally written in Aramaic, and xxxvii–lxxi, lxxxiii–civ, and probably i–v in Hebrew. The original language of lxxii–lxxxii is still indeterminable, but the probability of an Aramaic original seems to be greater than that of a Hebrew.

*Chapters i–v. Probably from a Hebrew original.* These chapters do not come from the same author or period as vi–xxxvi.

v. 9 (G<sup>g</sup>) <note>Refers to the Greek fragment found at Gizeh.</note> ‘They shall not be punished (Ethiopic: *yitḥēzazu* = Greek: *kolasthēsontai*) all the days of their life.’ Since the Ethiopic version has ‘sin’ (*hamartōsin*) here, if the text in both cases is rightly transmitted, it is probable that <term>yikht'u <note>original: "יחטאו"</note></term> <note>The Hebrew verb for "they shall sin."</note> stood in the original, and that it was rendered by ‘sin’ in the text of the Greek translation and by ‘be punished’ in the margin, or vice versa. In the *Testament of Asher*, vi. 1, the converse appears to have happened and the translator to have rendered this Hebrew verb by ‘are punished’ instead of by ‘sin.’

Again in i. 9 ‘He cometh with myriads of holy ones’ the text reproduces the Massoretic <note>The authoritative Hebrew text of the Old Testament.</note> of Deuteronomy xxxiii. 2 (see note on i. 9) in reading <term>atha <note>original: "אתא"</note></term> <note>Hebrew for "he came."</note> = ‘he cometh,’ whereas the three Targums <note>Aramaic translations/paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, the Syriac, and Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> read <term>itto <note>original: "אתה"</note></term> <note>Hebrew for "with him."</note> = ‘with him.’ Here the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> diverges wholly. The reading ‘he came’ is recognized as original. The writer of this section of Enoch used the Hebrew text, and followed neither Version nor Targum in reproducing it. Presumably he wrote in Hebrew also. See also notes i. 9 on p. 10.

*Chapters vi–xxxvi.* It will be observed in the notes on these chapters that sometimes the Greek is retranslated into Hebrew and sometimes into Aramaic. The reason is that when they were written (in 1901–1902) I was still

He provides linguistic evidence from specific verses to show how translation errors between Hebrew and Greek suggest a Hebrew original for the opening chapters.</summary>

undecided as to which language was the original. The balance of evidence now appears to me to be in favour of the latter <note>referring to Aramaic</note>, and this is as follows:—

(*a*) *Aramaic words transliterated in the Greek.* In xviii. 8 *phouka* <note>original Greek: φουκά</note> = <term>puka</term> <note>original Aramaic: פוּכָא; a word for stibium or eye-paint</note>, in xxviii. 1 and xxix. 1 *mandobara* and *babdera* <note>original Greek: μανδοβαρά and βαβδηρά</note> = <term>midbara</term> <note>original Aramaic: מדברא; meaning 'the desert'</note>.¹

(*b*) *Aramaic constructions.* In xix. 2 we have the peculiar Greek "the women of them of the fallen angels" <note>original Greek: αἱ γυναῖκες αὐτῶν τῶν παραβάντων ἀγγέλων</note>. This is a literal reproduction of the Aramaic idiom <term>the women-of-them of the angels who sinned</term> <note>original Aramaic: נשיהון די מלאכיא די חטו</note>. The same construction recurs in the Ethiopic version in ix. 8 which = "they lay with them with the women" <note>original Greek: συνεκοיμήθησαν μετ' αὐτῶν μετὰ τῶν θηλειῶν</note> = <term>they lay with-them with the-women</term> <note>original Aramaic: שכיבו עמהון עם נשיא</note>. Here the Greek version of Syncellus <gloss>Gs</gloss>, it is true, has omitted "with the women." This omission may be due to the unintelligibility of the construction to a pure Greek scribe. It is possible, however, that Syncellus is right, which connects "among the women" <note>original Greek: ἐν ταῖς θηλείαις</note> with the next verb—"they lay with them and among the women they were defiled." But this is very unlikely; for the natural construction would be "they lay with the women and in them they were defiled." We have probably a third instance of this idiom in vi. 8 "these are the heads of them the ten" <note>original Greek: οὗτοί εἰσιν ἀρχαὶ αὐτῶν οἱ δέקה</note>, where "the ten" should be emended into "of the decades" with the Ethiopic. Then "heads of them of the decades" = <term>heads-of-them of-the-tens</term> <note>original Aramaic: ראשיחון דעסריא</note>. This Aramaic idiom has made its way into the Old Testament as in Canticles <note>Song of Solomon</note> iii. 7.

(*c*) *Some of the proper names with which word-plays <note>paronomasias</note> are connected postulate an Aramaic original.* Thus in the Greek of Syncellus viii. 3 we have "and the third taught the signs of the earth." Now "the third" in vi. 7 is *Arakiel* = <term>Arakiel</term> <note>original Aramaic: ארקיאל</note>, where <term>Ara'</term> <note>original Aramaic: ארק</note> is Aramaic for 'earth.' Again in Syncellus viii. 3 we have "and the twentieth taught the signs of the moon" (The Gizeh Greek manuscript <gloss>Gg</gloss> has *Seriel* "the leading of the moon"), where "the twentieth" according to Syncellus vi. 7 is *Sariel* = <term>Sahariel</term> <note>original Aramaic: סהריאל</note>. Here <term>Sahar</term> <note>original Aramaic: סהר</note> is Aramaic for 'moon.' Again in viii. 3 the "eighth" in "the eighth taught the observation of the air" is the Gizeh Greek *Ezekiel* (Syncellus *Zakiel*) = <term>Shachaqiel</term> <note>original Aramaic: שחקיאל</note>. <term>Shachaq</term> <note>original Aramaic: שחק; meaning 'sky' or 'cloud'</note> (= air), it is true, is Hebrew as well as Aramaic.

(*d*) *Occasionally the source of corruptions in the Greek can be detected by retranslation into Aramaic.* I can offer but a few instances of this nature; for though there are many passages which can be restored by retranslation into the original, the restoration can be made equally well in most passages by retranslation into either Hebrew or Aramaic. The evidence, therefore, in this section is not conclusive. It serves to prove, however, the thoroughly Semitic basis of our author.

x. 17 "their Sabbaths" <note>original Greek: τὰ σάββατα αὐτῶν</note>. Here we should have "their old age." Here, as the note in its place shows, the source of the corruption is explicable both in Hebrew and Aramaic.

Since <term>ge</term>, however, is here used as a proper name, as denoting the 'Valley of Hinnom' <note>Gehenna</note>, its use may be justifiable in an Aramaic document.

**xii. 6** "there shall be no† mercy for them." <note>original: "οὐκ ἔσται αὐτοῖς εἰς ἔλεον"</note> See note on this passage on p. 238.

**xiii. 2** "there shall be no forbearance or †request for you regarding the wrongs you have shown," <note>original: "ἀνοχὴ καὶ ἐρώτησίς σοι οὐκ ἔσται περὶ ὧν ἔδειξας ἀδικημάτων"</note> 'no forbearance nor †request shall be to thee in regard to &c.' Here the word for "request" <note>original Hebrew: שְׁאֵלָא; Greek: ἐρώτησις</note> was a corruption for the word for "forgiveness" <note>original Hebrew: שֵׁלְוָא; Greek: ἄφεσις</note> <note>Footnote 1: Or possible "rest" <note>original Aramaic: שִׁלְוָא</note>.</note>. Compare xii. 5 "and there shall be no . . peace nor forgiveness." Here the Hebrew can also account for the corruption.

**xiii. 9** "mourning in Abel-si'ail" <note>original: "πενθοῦντες ἐν 'Αβελσιαήλ"</note> (so the Ethiopic version), that is, Abilene <note>original: "'Αβειλήνη"</note> = "Abilin in Abilene" <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: אבלין באבילין</note>—a <term>paronomasia|a play on words or a pun</term>.

**xiv. 6** "there shall be no †benefit to you from them, but they shall fall . . . by the sword." <note>original: "οὐκ ἔσται ὑμῖν ὄνησις αὐτῶν ἀλλὰ πεσοῦνται . . . ἐν μαχαίρᾳ"</note> Here "benefit" <note>original Greek: ὄνησις</note> = "remnant" or "excess," <note>original Hebrew: מוֹתָר</note> which should here have been rendered "remnant." <note>original Greek: κατάλειμμα</note> In Hebrew the word *yeter* <note>original: יתר</note> also admits of both senses.

**xiv. 8** "they were in haste and †were troubled." <note>original: "κατεσπούδαζον καὶ ἐθορύβαζον"</note> Here the second verb is impossible, and we have probably two renderings of one and the same Hebrew word *yibahalu* <note>original: יבהלו</note> accordingly as it is pointed as a <term>niphal|a Hebrew verb stem usually indicating passive or reflexive action</term> or a <term>piel|a Hebrew verb stem usually indicating intensive action</term> verb. In Aramaic the <term>pael|the intensive verb stem in Aramaic, equivalent to the Hebrew Piel</term> of this verb = "to trouble," "to disturb," or "to throw into confusion" <note>original Greek: θορυβάζω, ταράσσω, or συνταράσσω</note> in Daniel iv. 2, 16; v. 6, 10; vii. 15, 28, and is rendered by Theodotion <note>Footnote 2: Two manuscripts of Theodotion’s text (A and Q) render this as "to hasten," <note>original Greek: κατασπεύδω</note> but this may be owing to the influence of the Septuagint.</note> by one or other of the latter two verbs. On the other hand the <term>LXX|The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</term> renders the same Aramaic verb by "to hasten" <note>original Greek: κατασπεύδω</note> <note>Footnote 3: The translator of 2 Chronicles xxvi. 20; xxxv. 21 renders the Hebrew *behal* <note>original: בהל</note> by "to hasten" <note>original Greek: κατασπεύδω</note>.</note> in iv. 16 and v. 6. Thus the translator of the Septuagint, who, as we know from the rest of his translation of the Aramaic section of Daniel, was very familiar with Aramaic, assigns to the intensive form of the Aramaic verb the same meaning as the intensive and causative forms of the Hebrew. Hence we may assume that the intensive form in Aramaic could mean "to hasten" or "to trouble." Thus we could explain our text as a <term>dittographical|a scribal error where a letter, word, or phrase is written twice</term> rendering of one and the same Aramaic verb.

If there were two verbs in the original, and this is possible, then we have simply a mistranslation of the word *behal* <note>original: בהל</note> in the phrase "were troubled."

**xvi. 1** "from which . . . from the soul of their flesh" <note>original: "ἀφ’ ὧν . . . ἐκ τῆς ψυχῆς τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῶν"</note> = "which [is] from the soul of their flesh." <note>original Aramaic: די מנפש בשרהון</note> Similar Aramaic idioms are found also in xxii. 9; xxxii. 3. These anomalous Greek constructions can also be explained from a Hebrew background. In xxii. 6 "wherefore" <note>original Greek: διό</note> in "wherefore thus his voice" should with the Ethiopic version be emended into "whose" <note>original Greek: οὗ</note> in accordance with this idiom. Thus we should have 'whose voice thus.'

**xvii. 7.** Here the Ethiopic version = "the mountains of the darkness" <note>original Greek: τὰ ὄρη τῶν γνόφων</note> = "mountains of darkness" <note>original Aramaic: טורי קבלא</note> (see my note *in the relevant place*).

The phrase seems to be borrowed from Jeremiah 13:16. If this is so, then the Greek manuscript G^g, which reads "the winds of the darkness" <note>original Greek: τοὺς ἀνέμους τῶν γνόφων</note> = "winds of darkness" <note>original Aramaic: רוחי קבלא</note>. In that case we might suppose that the Greek translator found one word in the text and the other in the margin of his Semitic manuscript and rendered both, and that G^g preserved one and the Greek ancestor of the Ethiopic version (E) the other. The text in verse 9, where the Ethiopic equals "they shall be punished" (or "judged") <note>original Greek: κολασθήσονται or κριθήσονται</note> and G^g reads "they may sin" <note>original Greek: ἁμάρτωσιν</note> (which are two possible renderings of the same Hebrew word), requires a similar assumption.

**xxviii. 2** "full of trees and from the † seeds." <note>original Greek: πλήρης δένδρων καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν † σπερμάτων</note> It would be absurd to speak of a plain as full of ‘trees and seeds.’ Here I take "from the seeds" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν σπερμάτων</note> = "from seeds" <note>original Aramaic: מזרעין</note>, a corruption for "and of vegetables" <note>original Aramaic: ירעונין</note>. See my note in the specific location for other possible explanations.

**xxix. 2** † "trees of judgment." <note>original Greek: κρίσεως δένδρα</note> Here "of judgment" <note>original Greek: κρίσεως</note> = "of judgment" <note>original Aramaic: דרייא</note>, a corruption for "of fragrance" <note>original Aramaic: דריחא</note> (so Praetorius) = "fragrant" <note>original Greek: εὐώδη</note>. In Hebrew the corruption can be explained equally well.

**xxxi. 3** "when they rub." <note>original Greek: ὅταν τρίβωσιν</note> These words refer to certain fragrant trees mentioned in the preceding verse. These trees yielded (see p. 70, note 35) a fragrant odor when burnt. Hence it is possible that the Aramaic "they shall rub" <note>original Aramaic: ידקון</note> is corrupt for "they shall burn" <note>original Aramaic: ילקון</note> = "they may burn" <note>original Greek: καύσωσιν</note>. Thus: ‘when they burn it, it is more fragrant etc.’

### *Chapters 37-70, from a Hebrew original.* 
The assumption of a Hebrew original is required by some of the following passages, while others would admit of either Hebrew or Aramaic.

**xl. 9** ‘The third who is set over all the powers is Gabriel.’ There is a <term>paronomasia</term> <note>A play on words or a pun, often used in ancient texts to link a person's name to their function.</note> here on Gabriel’s name—"He who is over all powers is Gabriel" <note>original Hebrew: אשר על כל גבורות הוא גבריאל; note the play between 'Gevurot' (powers) and 'Gabriel'</note>. This wordplay is possible also in Aramaic. In the same verse the words ‘the second, who is set over all the diseases . . . of the sons of men, is Raphael’ = "He who is over all the sicknesses of the sons of men is Raphael" <note>original Hebrew: אשר על כל מהלות בני אדם הוא רפאל</note>, contain a reference to the derivation of the name Raphael, which is possible only in Hebrew—"Rapha" <note>original Hebrew: רפא</note> ‘to heal.’

**xlv. 3** ‘On that day thine Elect One will sit on the throne of glory
And *he will choose their works*.’
The words in italics are a translation of the Ethiopic <note>original Ethiopic: የኀሪ፡ ምግባሪሆሙ፡</note>. Flemming, after the example of his predecessors, translates: ‘will make a choice among their works.’ But this is a mistranslation and would require a different preposition <note>original Ethiopic: እምግባሪሆሙ፡</note>. Moreover it is absurd to boot. The source of the corruption becomes clear on retranslation. Thus "he will choose" <note>original Ethiopic: የኀሪ፡</note> = "he will choose" <note>original Greek: ἐκλέξεται</note> = the Hebrew "he will choose" <note>original Hebrew: יבחר</note>, which might (compare Isaiah 48:10) itself equal "he will test" <note>original Greek: δοκιμάσει</note>, or else it is a corruption...

of the word *will try* <note>original Hebrew: יבחן (yibchan)</note>, which normally means ‘will try.’ Thus we should read ‘And he will try their works.’ In Aramaic the word *try* <note>original: בחן (bchan)</note> has both meanings. Hence this passage is indecisive.

xlvi. 4^b ‘ He will † raise up the kings and the mighty from their thrones.’ Of this verse a double-writing <term>dittograph: a scribal error where a passage is accidentally repeated</term> occurs four lines later, xlvi. 5^a :

> ‘And he will put down kings from their thrones and kingdoms,’

for the parallelism shows that the latter is an intrusion. On the other hand, the Ethiopic *he will put down* <note>original: ይገፍትሖሙ</note> = the Greek *he will take down* <note>original: καθαιρήσει</note> = the Hebrew *he will remove* <note>original: יסיר (yasir)</note> is right (cf. 2 Chronicles 30:14), whereas the Ethiopic *he will raise up* <note>original: ይነሥኦሙ</note> = the Greek *he will awaken* <note>original: ἐγερεῖ</note> = the Hebrew *he will stir up* <note>original: יעיר (ya'ir)</note> is wrong.^1 The word *stir up* <note>original: יעיר</note> would then be a corruption for *remove* <note>original: יסיר</note>.

lii. 9 ‘ All these things will be † denied and destroyed from the face of the earth.’ Here Dillmann and Flemming try to give a better sense to the passage by rendering the Ethiopic *they will be denied* <note>original: ይትሐሐዱ</note> as: ‘will disappear’ <note>original German: "werden verschwinden"</note> and Beer as ‘will be annihilated’ <note>original German: "werden vernichtet werden"</note>. But the word is unexampled in these senses in Ethiopic. The explanation is discoverable through retranslation. The Ethiopic = the Greek *they will be denied and they will be made to disappear* <note>original: ἀπαρνηθήσονται καὶ ἀφανισθήσονται</note>. These two verbs are double-renderings <note>dittographic</note> of the single Hebrew word *they will be destroyed* <note>original: יכחדו (yikachadu)</note>.

lvi. 7 ‘ Till the number of their corpses is † through their death †.’ The Ethiopic *from their death* <note>original: እምሞቶሙ</note> = the Greek *from their death* <note>original: ἐκ θανάτου αὐትῶν</note> = the Hebrew *from their death* <note>original: ממותם</note>, which is a corruption for *more than myriads* <note>original: מרבות</note>.

lxv. 10 ‘ Their judgment has been determined upon and will not be † reckoned before me.’ Here ‘will not be reckoned before me’ = the Greek *it will not be reckoned before my face* <note>original: οὐ λογισθήσεται κατὰ πρόσωπόን μου</note> = the Hebrew *it will not be reckoned from before* <note>original: לא יחשב מפני</note> where the verb is corrupt for *it will be withheld* <note>original: יחשך</note> used of judgments and calamities. Thus the text = ‘their judgment has been determined up and will not be withheld by Me.’ This restoration is possible also through Aramaic.

lxv. 10 ‘ Because of the † months which they have searched out and through which they know &c.’ Here Halévy (*Journal of the Asiatic Society*, 374-375, 1867) objects that the Ethiopic word <note>original: አውራኅ</note> signifies ‘months’ and never astrology, and that the knowledge of the future could not have been regarded as criminal by the authors of Enoch. Hence he conjectures that the Hebrew word for *months* <note>original: חדשים (chadashim)</note> was a corruption of the word for *sorceries* <note>original: חרשים (charashim)</note>. This conjecture restores sanity to the text.

lxv. 11 ‘ For these there will be no place of † refuge for ever.’ Here the Ethiopic *refuge* <note>original: ምግባአ</note> = the Greek *turning back* <note>original: ἀποστሮφή</note> = the Hebrew *return* <note>original: תשובה (teshuvah)</note>, which should here have been rendered ‘repentance.’

lxvii. 13 ‘ These waters of judgment minister to the healing of the

---

^1 In the notes in that location I have supposed the Hebrew words *he will cast down* <note>original: יפיל</note> and *he will take away* <note>original: יטול</note>.

body of the † angels. Here, as Halévy <note>Joseph Halévy (1827–1917), a French-Jewish Orientalist and traveler</note> (pp. 366–367) has remarked, ‘angels’ is an impossible reading. It = <note>original Hebrew: mal’akhim</note> ‘angels,’ corrupt for <note>original Hebrew: melakhim</note> ‘kings.’

lxix. 13 ‘This is the † number of Kesbeêl.’ The word ‘number’ is here unintelligible. The context requires some such words as ‘office,’ ‘function.’ Halévy’s explanation is very satisfactory. He holds that the translator here rendered <note>original Hebrew: pequdah</note> by ‘number’ when he should have given ‘charge,’ ‘function.’

From the above restorations on the basis of a Hebrew original, the majority of which are not possible on the hypothesis of an Aramaic original, the natural conclusion is that the chapters xxxvii–lxx were originally written in Hebrew.

### *Chapters lxxii—lxxxii. From Hebrew most probably.*

lxxvii. 1 ‘The first † wind is called the east because it is the first : and the second the south because the Most High † descends there.’ We have here two <term>paronomasias</term> <note>wordplays or puns</note>, one misrendering and one corruption. First of all, as Halévy points out, the Greek translator erred by rendering <note>original Hebrew: ruach</note> by ‘wind’ instead of by ‘quarter.’ Cf. Ezekiel xlii. 20. Next, ‘Most High descends’ = <note>original Hebrew: yered ram</note>, corrupt for <note>original Hebrew: yadur ram</note> = ‘the Most High abides,’ a play on <note>original Hebrew: darom</note> ‘south.’ Finally, the ‘east’ = <note>original Hebrew: qedem</note> : hence it is ‘the first’ <note>original Hebrew: qadmoni</note>. In verses 2, 3 there are similar wordplays.

lxxviii. 1. See note 13.
lxxviii. 2. See note 25.
lxxx. 5. See note 1.

### *Chapters lxxxiii—xc, from Hebrew (or Aramaic?).* The evidence is here very scanty as yet.

lxxxiii. 11. Here a corruption in text can be emended by retranslation into Greek or Hebrew. See note in loc. <note>Latin: in loco, meaning 'in the place' or 'in the relevant note'</note>

xc. 18 **covered over them** <note>original Ethiopic: kadana dibehomu</note> = covered over them <note>original Greek: ekalypsen ep’ autous</note>, a clear <term>Hebraism</term> <note>an idiom or construction derived from Hebrew</note> = covered over them <note>original Hebrew: kissah aleihem</note>. See my note 16 on p. 185.

xc. 38 ‘The first . . . became a † word.’ Here E <note>the Ethiopic version</note> = word <note>original Greek: rhēma</note>, but the Greek was not ‘word’ but *rēm*—a transliteration of <note>original Hebrew: re’em</note> = ‘buffalo.’ If we were sure that ‘word’ <note>original Greek: rhēma</note> stood originally in the Greek translation it would be an argument in favour of an Aramaic original ; for ‘word’ would = <note>original Aramaic: reima</note>.

## The Book of Enoch

<note>original: "መጽሐፈ፡ ሄኖክ፡" (Maṣḥafa Hēnok). This is an ancient Jewish religious work, traditionally ascribed to Enoch, the great-grandfather of Noah. While it is excluded from the Western biblical canon, it is preserved in its entirety only in the Ge'ez language of Ethiopia.</note>

# The Book of Enoch: II. 1—IV.

II. Observe <note>original: ጠይቁ (ṭayyequ). The editor notes this corresponds to the Greek κατανοήሳτε (katanoēsate), meaning "examine closely" or "consider."</note> everything that takes place in the heaven, how they do not change their orbits, and the luminaries <note>original: ብርሃናት (berhānāt)</note> which are in the heaven, how they all rise and set in order, each in its own season, and they do not transgress against their appointed order. 2. Behold the earth, and give heed to the things which take place upon it from first to last, how no work of God fails to appear <note>original: ያስተርኢ (yāstar’i). The editor suggests this may be a mistranslation of the original Greek 'appears' or 'is manifest.'</note> in its unchanging order. 3. Behold summer and winter, how the whole earth is filled with water, and clouds and dew and rain rest upon it.

III. Observe and see how all the trees appear as though they were withered and all their leaves have fallen, except for fourteen <note>original: ፲ወ፬ (14)</note> trees which do not lose their foliage but retain the old until the new comes after two or three winters.

IV. And again, observe the days of summer, how the sun is upon the earth over against it. And you seek for shelter and shade because of the heat of the sun, and the earth also burns with growing heat <note>original: እምቆ (em-qo). Variants in the notes suggest "from the heat" or "scorching."</note>...

2. *qu, t² β. g t¹* read *they do not change*. *m* reads *they do not come* (sic).

16. = *appears*. This is probably a wrong rendering of the original, see note 3, p. 7.

<header>II. 1—III. ENOCH 7</header>

## II. Observe all the works in heaven, how they do not change their paths, <insert>and</insert> the luminaries that are in heaven, how they all rise and set, each one appointed in its appointed time, <insert>and they appear in their festivals,</insert> and they do not transgress their own order. 2. Behold the earth and consider the works being done in it from the beginning until the completion, <insert>how they are perishable,</insert> <note>original: "ὡς εἰσιν φθαρτά"</note> how <insert>nothing of the things upon the earth</insert> changes, <insert>but</insert> all the works of God appear <insert>to you</insert>. 3. Behold the summer and the winter . . . ## III. Examine and see all the trees, <margin>III. 1b—V. 1a lost through <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <note>A scribal error where the eye skips from one word to a similar ending later in the text, causing a loss of words.</note></margin>

parallel columns. That the Latin are versions of Enoch chapter 1, verse 9 and not of Jude 14, 15 was shown by Zahn in 1890. The words, *And to destroy all the impious*, *And to convict all flesh* <note>original Latin: "Et perdere omnes impios, Et arguere omnem carnem"</note> furnish irrefutable proof of this view.

This being presumed we have to determine the relative faithfulness of the Versions. First of all it is clear that Jude is the least original as it compresses the two clauses (*b*) and (*c*) into one, and introduces <term>Lord</term> <note>original Greek: "κύριος"</note> after <term>he came</term> <note>original Greek: "ἦλθεν"</note>. Next the Pseudo-Vigilius <note>An anonymous author whose works were formerly attributed to Vigilius.</note> is defective: phrases are wanting in (*a*) and the entire clause (*β*) is omitted. The Pseudo-Cyprian is the most perfect of the three as regards the parallelism, though corrupt in "of his messengers" <note>original Latin: "nuntiorum" = Greek: "ἀγγέλων" (angels)</note>, "God" <note>Latin: "Deo"</note> for "him" <note>Latin: "eo"</note>, and wanting in "impious" after "sinners." Turning now to the Greek manuscript <note>referred to as "G"</note> we see that it agrees in form with the Pseudo-Cyprian and Pseudo-Vigilius, save that against all authorities it adds after <term>words</term> <note>original Greek: "λόγων"</note> a clause, which is obviously a <term>dittography</term> <note>A scribal error where a letter or phrase is accidentally written twice.</note>. The interpolation in the first line is noticed in the text. Thus the structure is well established: *namely, three clauses (a), (b), (c), the last of which is subdivided into two (α) and (β).*

On the other hand the infinitives *to destroy* <note>Latin: "perdere" = Greek: "ἀπολέσαι"</note> and *to convict* <note>Latin: "arguere" = Greek: "ἐλέγξαι"</note> are right, and this evidence, together with the Ethiopic version <note>referred to as "E"</note>, shows that we should not read <term>he will destroy</term> <note>Greek: "ἀπολέσει"</note> and <term>he will convict</term> <note>Greek: "ἐλέγξει"</note> in the Greek but <term>to destroy</term> and <term>to convict</term>. The parallelism also supports this view.

Having now ascertained the structure and details of the text we approach the Ethiopic and find that it *preserves all the clauses*, though in the case of (*b*) and (*β*) defectively, and of (*a*) corruptly and defectively. Thus it omits <term>all</term> <note>Greek: "πάντας"</note> in (*b*) and <term>and of the hard words which they spoke</term> <note>Greek: "καὶ σκληρῶν ὧν ἐλάλησαν λόγων"</note> in (*β*).

We conclude, therefore, that the original form is to be rendered as follows in English :

> I. 9. Behold! He comes with His holy myriads
> ->(a) To execute judgment upon all,<-
> ->(b) And to destroy all the ungodly,<-
> ->(c) And to convict all flesh<-
> ->(α) Of all their works of ungodliness which they have ungodly committed,<-
> ->(β) And of all the hard things which ungodly sinners have spoken against Him.<-

---

¹ Supplied by Swete. ² So Dillmann and Radermacher from <gloss>they will jump</gloss> <note>original: "αλλουνται"</note>. Cf. <gloss>they changed</gloss> <note>original: "ηλλυοσαν"</note> in verse 1 for <term>they changed</term> <note>original: "ἠλλοίωσαν"</note>. ³ <gloss>and it is seen/suited</gloss> <note>Hebrew: "וראוי"</note> = 'suited' : cf. Esther ii. 9 ; id. vi. 4 for this meaning. At any rate <term>appears</term> <note>Greek: "φαίνεται"</note> gives no appropriate sense. ⁴ III. 1b—V. 1a lost through <term>homoeoteleuton</term>.

And they began to go in <note>original: "ይባኡ"</note> unto them and were defiled <note>original: "ተደመሩ"; the translator notes this may be a corruption of a Greek term meaning "to be defiled"</note> with them, and they taught them sorcery and incantations, and the cutting of roots, and made them acquainted with plants. <note>The translator notes that the Ge'ez "ዕፀው" here refers to medicinal or magical herbs/shrubs, similar to the Hebrew "עץ" used in the Book of Noah.</note> 2. And the women became pregnant, and they bare large giants, and their stature was each three thousand <note>The text reads 70,000 in some versions, but the translator notes a variant for 300.</note> cubits. 3. VIII. And Azazel taught men to make swords, and knives, and shields, and to see what was behind them <note>original: "ዘእምድኅሬሆሙ"; likely a corruption of the Greek word for "metals"</note>, and the works of bracelets and ornaments, and the use of antimony <note>eye-paint</note>, and the beautifying of the eyebrows, and every kind of costly stones, and all coloring tinctures.

### Critical Notes

1. *q* reads **they commit sin.** 2. Possibly corrupt for **they were defiled** = Greek *miainesthai*. 3. *m* adds **also**. 4. Various manuscripts read **seven** or **men**. 5. *g q t^1, n y*. So Greek *tas botanas* (the plants). *m* reads **wood.** *u, t^2* read **plants.** Here **plants** is a rendering of *botanas* as in *Wisdom of Solomon* xvi. 12, and must be translated ‘plants’ or ‘shrubs,’ as in *Jubilees* x. 12. We have this use of the Hebrew word for "tree/wood" in the Hebrew Book of Noah which treats of the subject in our text: **"The angel showed how to heal with the plants (or shrubs) of the earth."** 6. *q* reads **they taught them.** 7. *m* reads **mighty giants.** 8. *m* reads **three hundred.** 9. *m, f.* All other manuscripts read **until.** 10. Corrupt for **until**, a rendering of the Greek article *tous*. 11. = **so that**. Corrupt for **but when**. Read **and he asked.** 12. *n x* read **they asked.** 13. Various manuscript divisions regarding the word for **sustenance**. 14. The **and** may have arisen through a misreading of the Greek. **They turned** = *etrapēsan*, which seems preferable to *etolmēsan* (they dared) in the Greek version. 15. *q* = Greek **and they were devouring**. 17. *q* reads **and they turned.** 19. The manuscripts are strangely divided between **they were devoured** and **they devoured**. We require a form representing the practice of the giants. 21. Bracketed as a duplicate of **then**. 24. *g.* Other manuscripts read **against the lawless.** 25. *n* reads **swords.** 26. *g t u* read **knives.** 27. *g q u* read **and they see.** 30. = **the things after them**, corrupt for the Greek word for **metals**. 31. *q, t^2 e.* Other manuscripts read **and their works.** 33. *q* reads **and they were painted.** 35. This together with the preceding word = **the beautifying of the eyelids**. 36. = **of all kinds**.

# IX. 5-9. ENOCH

## Version $G^g$ <note>The Akhmim Fragment, a Greek manuscript discovered in Egypt in 1886.</note>

5. And ⌈now behold⌉ the daughters

---

$^1$ $G^g$ = of all. $^2$ $G^g$ omits through a copying error <note>term: hmt. (homoeoteleuton); a scribal error where the eye skips from one word to a similar ending later in the text</note> "and there is nothing that can be hidden from You. You see" which is present in the Ethiopic ($E$) and $G^s$. $^3$ See note 10, p. 22. $^4$ The Ethiopic version ($E$) presupposes exactly this impossible text except that it reads "he knew" or "he made known" for "they knew." If we insert "and" before "they knew" as some scholars suggest, the sense is unsatisfactory. Since $G^s$ reads "to know," it may be best to read "to know" (Greek: *gnōnai*) here and view the error as native to the $G^g$ manuscript. This gives the sense "which men were trying to know." Alternatively, if we take the meaning "to practice," the text might be a corruption of a Hebrew word meaning "and they are perishing." This fits the theme that men are being destroyed by this forbidden knowledge. $^5$ Add "among the females" following the Ethiopic and $G^s$ versions. $^6$ $G^s$ = and. $^7$ See note 1 above. $^8$ See note 2 above. $^9$ $E$ and $G^g$ = "and he revealed the mysteries of the world." $^{10}$ Here $G^s$ means "they practice (Azazel’s) practices in order to know the mysteries." This is possible, but unlikely. $^{11}$ Corrupt text. $E$ and $G^g$ = "And Semjaza." $^{12}$ Corrupt for "to rule."

# The Book of Enoch
### X. 16—XII. 1.

...the work <note>original: ግብረ (gibra)</note> of righteousness and truth shall be a plant <note>The metaphor of a "plant" or "planting" is frequently used in Enoch to describe the community of the righteous.</note> for eternity in joy. 17. And now all the righteous shall escape, and they shall live until they beget a thousand children, and they shall complete all the days of their youth and their sabbaths <margin>from sin</margin> in peace. 18. And in those days the whole earth shall be tilled in righteousness, and all of it shall be planted with trees and be filled with blessing. 19. And all the trees of desire shall be planted on it, and they shall plant vines on it; and the vine which is planted on it shall yield wine in abundance, and every seed which is sown on it, each measure <note>original: መስፈርተ (masfarta)</note> shall yield a thousand, and each measure of olives shall yield ten presses <term>presses: specifically a "bath" or "ephah" measure for oil</term> of oil. 20. And you, cleanse the earth from all oppression, and from all unrighteousness, and from all sin, and from all godlessness, and from all the uncleanness that is wrought upon the earth; destroy them from off the face of the earth. 21. And let all the children of men become righteous, and let all nations offer adoration and praise Me, and all shall worship Me. 22. And the earth shall be cleansed from all corruption, and from all sin, and from all plague, and from all suffering; and I will never again send a flood <note>literally: "I will not repeat to send [it]"</note> upon it, from generation to generation and forever. 

XI. And in those days I will open the storehouses of blessing which are in heaven, so as to bring them down upon the earth, upon the work and upon the labor of the children of men. 2. And peace and truth shall be partners throughout all the days of the world and throughout all the generations of men. 

XII. Before these things...
