<header>Chapters 17—12:1. ENOCH 31</header>

# ENOCH

17. And now all the righteous shall escape, and they shall live until they beget thousands, and all the days of their youth and <note>original: "their sabbaths"</note> their old age <note>The Greek text literally says "sabbaths," but scholars believe this is a mistranslation of a Hebrew word for "old age." See marginal note 1.</note> they shall fulfill in peace. 18. Then all the earth shall be tilled in righteousness, and a tree shall be planted in it, and it shall be filled with blessing. 19. And all the trees of the earth shall rejoice <note>The text here is difficult; see marginal note 3 regarding "trees of joy."</note> and be planted, and they shall plant vines, and the vine which they plant shall produce thousands of pitchers of wine; and for every measure of seed it shall produce <note>a thousandfold</note>, and of olives it shall produce ten baths <term>bath: an ancient liquid measure, roughly 22 liters</term> per measure. 20. And you, cleanse the earth from all impurity and from all unrighteousness and from all sin and impiety, and wipe away all the impurities that are happening upon the earth. 21. And all the peoples shall be worshippers, and all shall bless me and bow down. 22. And the whole earth shall be cleansed from every defilement and from all impurity and wrath and scourge, and I will never again send these upon them for all the generations of eternity. XI. And then I will open the storehouses of blessing which are in heaven, to bring them down upon the works, upon the labor of the sons of men. 2. And then truth and peace shall be joined together for all the days of eternity and for all the generations of men.

XII. Before these words Enoch was taken away, and no one of the children of men <note>knew where he was hidden.</note>

***

<margin>1. A Hebrew word for "sabbaths" was likely misread or wrongly vocalized for "old age." The error is explainable in Hebrew where *shubatam* was written instead of *sebatam*. Therefore, read "their old age." 2. This appears to be used in a sense where the subjects complete their own time. The Ethiopic version renders it differently. 3. Corrupt text. I cannot restore the original wording. "Tree of joy" (as in the Ethiopic) is an expression not found elsewhere. The Greek "all the trees of the earth shall rejoice" might be a corruption of a Hebrew phrase meaning "goodly in appearance." Both the Greek and Ethiopic versions seem damaged here. 4. The text is translatable but seems corrupt. The Ethiopic version suggests each measure of seed will produce thousands. 5. The Ethiopic version reads "unrighteousness." 6. The Ethiopic adds "all." 7. The Ethiopic adds "from the earth" and "and all the sons of men shall be righteous." 8. The Ethiopic adds "upon the earth." 9. The Ethiopic transposes these words. 10. The Ethiopic reads "of the ages," a wrong expansion of the shorthand for "men" appearing in the Greek.</margin>

***

# XIV. 3-8. ENOCH

<page-num>37</page-num>

...the sons of heaven. 4. I wrote out your petition <insert>the angels'</insert> <note>original: τῶν ἀγγέλων</note>, and in my vision this was shown to me: and neither was your petition accepted, 5. so that you might no longer ascend into heaven for all the ages; and it was commanded to bind you in the <term>bonds of the earth</term> <note>original: δεσμοῖς τῆς γῆς; see note 6 below regarding a likely scribal error for "prisoners of the earth"</note> for all the generations of the world. 6. And <insert>that</insert> before these things you shall see the destruction of your beloved sons, and that you shall have no pleasure in them, but they shall fall before you by the sword. 7. And your petition concerning them shall not be granted, nor concerning yourselves—even though you are weeping and praying and not speaking any word from the writing which I wrote. 8. And to me a vision was thus shown: behold, clouds in the vision were calling me and mists were crying out to me, and the courses of the stars and the lightnings were hurrying me and <term>disturbing</term> <note>original: ἐθορύβαζόν; likely a mistranslation of a word meaning "hastened"</note> me, and winds in my vision <term>caused me to fly</term> <note>original: ἐξεπέτασάν; literally "spread out," but used here in a sense of flight</note>...

---

¹ A gloss. The Ethiopic version (E) omits it. ² E reads "according to this." ³ E reads "that." ⁴ E reads "it shall not be for you for all the days of the age, and the judgment has been completed upon you and it shall not be for you." ⁵ E reads "and from now on." ⁶ For <term>bonds</term> <note>original: δεσμοῖς</note> we should probably read <term>prisoners</term> <note>original: δεσμίοις</note>. The phrase is found in Lamentations 3:33 <note>Hebrew: אסיρι ארץ</note>, Septuagint <term>prisoners of the earth</term>. The phrase here means 'those confined in the earth.' For similar phrases see Zechariah 9:11, 12; Wisdom of Solomon 17:2. There was an obvious <term>wordplay</term> <note>original: paronomasia</note> between "prisoners" and "to imprisonment" <note>Hebrew: אסורי למאסר</note>, for the Greek as early as Origen's time had "bonds." But Origen's words (*Against Celsus* v. 52) "to be punished, having been cast into bonds in the earth" show that he could make nothing of "bonds of the earth." The corruption most probably arose in the Aramaic "prisoners of the earth" <note>אסיρι ארעא</note> being mistaken for "bonds of the earth" <note>אסורי ארעא</note>. E is defective, reading simply "in the earth." ⁷ E reads "days." ⁸ The manuscript reads "concerning." ⁹ Beer (Kautzsch, *Apocrypha* ii. 245) regards this word as a rendering of a Hebrew word meaning "the remnant" <note>יתר</note>, which, however, the translator rendered by <term>pleasure/profit</term> <note>ὄνησις</note>. But could "pleasure" be a rendering of "remnant"? Since E is here corrupt but points to "remnant" (see note 23, p. 36), the original Aramaic was probably <note>מותר</note>, which can mean either "remnant" or "profit." ¹⁰ We should expect "and of those weeping." ¹¹ Emended from the manuscript's "not," which E follows. The corruption of "not" <note>μή</note> into "truly/verily" <note>μήν</note> is found in chapter 10:7. If, however, the negative is original, "not speaking" may be a corruption for "not obtaining" or "not receiving" <note>לא מקבלין</note>, which should be taken as the main conclusion: 'Ye are not to receive.' ¹² E reads "vision." ¹³ This word (= <term>they were disturbing</term>, and so E) cannot be right. We require a synonym of <term>they were hurrying me</term>. Now "they were disturbing" <note>ἐθορύβαζον</note> corresponds to the Hebrew <note>בהלו</note>. In this context the translator should have rendered it <term>they hastened</term>. In Aramaic this verb is only found in the sense of "to hurry" in an intransitive way, but this may be an accident. ¹⁴ This may be an attempt to render an Aramaic word meaning "caused to fly" <note>אפרחו</note>. This Aramaic verb is used by the Targum of Onkelos to render "brought" or "drove" in Numbers 11:31. On the other hand, the Septuagint gives "passed through" but one manuscript gives "spread out" (as already remarked by Lods in this passage). Now if "caused to fly" stood in the original, "spread out" <note>ἐξεπέτασαν</note> may have been an attempted rendering. But in that case we must attach to it a meaning that cannot be justified in Greek. This verb is from <term>to spread out</term> <note>ἐκπετάννυμι</note>, but the translator of E apparently confused it with "they flew out" and derived it from <term>to fly out</term> <note>ἐκπέταμαι</note> and ascribed to it an active meaning.

meaning, i. e. ‘to cause to fly.’ The same wrong meaning is attached to "he spread out" <note>original: ἐξεπέτασε</note> by the Ethiopic translator of Proverbs 13:16. On the whole I am inclined to regard "they spread out" <note>original: ἐξεπέτασαν</note> here as a corruption of "they passed through" <note>original: ἐξεπέρασαν</note>, as Lods suggests. The idea seems to be derived from Numbers 11:31 "a wind from the Lord and it brought across <note>original: ἐξεπέρασεν</note> quail."

<margin>
1. Ethiopic = "they hurried me," or possibly "they lifted."
2. Ethiopic wrongly translates into the next clause.
3. Ethiopic = "of a building" (participle).
4. Manuscript reads "of a tongue" (singular).
5. = **stones of hail** <note>Hebrew: אֲבְנֵי בָרָד</note> (Isaiah 30:30).
6. Ethiopic = "in stones made of snow."
7. Ethiopic prefixes "and."
8. Ethiopic = "delight." These words are frequently confused: cf. Genesis 49:20. It is difficult to decide which is original. "Nourishment" <note>original: τροφή</note> may be right. On the other hand "delight" <note>original: τρυφή</note> is used of the Grave <note>Sheol</note> in Sirach 14:16 "it is not possible to seek delight in the Grave" <note>Hebrew: לְבַקֵשׁ תַּעֲנוּג</note>. Cf. also Erubin 54a.
9. Added from Ethiopic.
10. Seems corrupt. Ethiopic which gives good sense = "another house larger than this and its whole door was opened before me and." The Greek manuscript appears to be a dislocated form of the Ethiopic.
11. Ethiopic = "and the."
12. Ethiopic adds "in it."
13. Certain Ethiopic manuscripts = "of a high (throne)."
14. Ethiopic = "its wheel was like a shining sun." The expression goes back to Daniel 7:9 "its wheels were burning fire" <note>Aramaic: גַּλְגִּלּוֹהִי נוּר דָּלִק</note>. The text of the Ethiopic is preferable as to sense.

<margin>3</margin> was corrupted into <term>Ananim</term> <note>Hebrew: עננין, meaning "clouds"</note>. Or "pasturing" <note>original: νεμόμενα</note> may in the sense of ‘pasturing’ be a rendering of <term>Ro'im</term> <note>Hebrew: רעין, "shepherds/pasturers"</note>, which being a corruption of <term>Re'e'in</term> <note>Hebrew: רעעין, "crushing/breaking"</note> (so Beer) was itself corrupted into <term>Ananim</term> = clouds. Bouriant followed by Flemming takes "clouds" to be a corruption of <term>Nephilim</term>. But "pasturing" is against this. <margin>4</margin> A <term>gloss</term> <note>A brief explanatory note or addition by a later scribe</note>. G<sup>g</sup> and the Ethiopic version <note>E</note> omit. <margin>5</margin> Ethiopic = tremblings <note>original: τρόμους</note>. <margin>6</margin> So also G<sup>s</sup>: Ethiopic omits. It may be a <term>doublet</term> <note>Two different translations of the same word appearing side-by-side</note> of "eating nothing." If it belongs to the original text it may be a mis-rendering of <term>Ra'ab</term> <note>Hebrew: רעב</note> = ‘to hunger,’ and should be replaced by "hungering," or better "famishing." To fast <note>original: ἀσιτεῖν</note> in the sense of an involuntary fast would be unusual. Beer quotes Wellhausen, *Remnants of Arabian Paganism*, 149 sq., to the effect that the <term>Jinns</term> <note>Spirits in Arabian mythology</note> suffer from a devouring hunger and yet cannot eat. <margin>7</margin> Ethiopic corrupt = invisible. See p. 44, note 22. <margin>8</margin> Manuscript wrongly transposed before "and shall rise up." <margin>9</margin> Ethiopic = against the women. <margin>10</margin> Add "of the giants" with G<sup>s</sup> and Ethiopic. It is required by "from whom." <margin>11</margin> "From whom" must be taken with "from the soul of their flesh." It is the <term>Semitic idiom</term> <note>A phrase structure typical of Hebrew or Aramaic</note> "from the soul of their flesh" <note>original: די מנפש בשרהון</note>. <margin>12</margin> Add with G<sup>s</sup> and Ethiopic "shall be called evil spirits." See note 1. <margin>13</margin> See note 6 above. <margin>14</margin> These words though not found in G<sup>g</sup> or Ethiopic may be genuine as Lods recognized. <margin>15</margin> See note 9 above. <margin>16</margin> A gloss from Genesis 6:4? <term>Nephilim</term> is a transliteration of the Hebrew <note>original: נפלים</note> and thus a doublet of "giants" going before: see Genesis 6:4. "The mighty ones of the earth" is an expanded rendering of <term>Ha-Gibborim</term> <note>Hebrew: הגברים, "the heroes/mighty men"</note> and "the great famous ones" of <term>Anshe Ha-Shem</term> <note>Hebrew: אנשי השם, "men of the name"</note> in the same verse.

<margin>
1. The Ethiopic version wrongly omits "judgment."
2. Add with the Syncellus fragment "it shall be consummated all at once together." The Ethiopic reads "it shall be completely consummated."
3. The Ethiopic adds "formerly."
4. Interpolated? The Ethiopic omits.
5. The Ethiopic reads "rejected" or "despised."
6. The Ethiopic adds "to you."
7. The Ethiopic uses a word for "whirlwind" or "tempest," as seen in the Greek translation of Job 27:20.
8. The Ethiopic reads "the peak of the head."
9. The Ethiopic seems corrupted here, but may refer back to "the extreme depths."
10. The Ethiopic adds "and a sword of fire."
11. The Ethiopic reads "receiving." I do not understand the word "providing" in this clause.
12. The Ethiopic reads "And I saw."
13. The Ethiopic omits this through a scribal error of skipping similar-looking words.
14. The Ethiopic reads "the mountains of the glooms"—a phrase derived from the Hebrew of Jeremiah 13:16 "mountains of twilight" where the Aramaic translation (Targum of Jonathan) has "mountains of darkness." In the original Hebrew/Aramaic, the word for "mountains" was likely corrupted into the word for "winds." These mountains are probably those which the Babylonian Cosmogony <note>Ancient Babylonian theory of the universe's origin</note> represents as standing at the ends of the earth near the "springs of the great deep."
15. The Ethiopic reads "waters of the entire abyss."

^1 The Ethiopic version reads "of the Lord." &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ^2 The manuscript reads "king" (nominative case). &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ^3 The Ethiopic version reads "eternal." &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ^4 The Ethiopic version transposes this after "holy place," and perhaps rightly. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ^5 The Ethiopic version reads "into the holy place and they shall take its fragrance," but, as we have shown (note 5, p. 64), it can by an easy emendation be brought into line with the Greek. # XXXII. 1–5. ENOCH 73

That tree is like the carob <note>original: "στροβιλέᾳ" - likely referring to a pine or cone-bearing tree, though the text compares the height to a pine and the leaves to a carob</note> in height, and its leaves are like the carob <note>original: "κερατίᾳ"</note>, and its fruit is like the clusters of the vine, very cheerful, and its fragrance reaches far from the tree. 5. ---

"He took him (Enoch) from the world, so that he might serve Him... From that time on, the book was handed down which is called the Book of Enoch. In the hour that God took him up, He showed him all the highest storehouses; He showed him the tree of life in the middle of the garden, its leaves and its branches." <note>Latin original: "tulit eum (Enochum) ex mundo..."</note> Again (vol. ii. Section *Beshalach* <note>original Hebrew: "בשלח" - a portion of the Torah</note>, p. 55$^a$): "In the book of Enoch it is narrated that the Holy and Blessed One, when He commanded him to ascend and showed him all the storehouses of the upper and lower kingdoms, showed him also the tree of life and the tree concerning which Adam received the commandment." <note>Latin original: "In Enochi libro narratur..."</note> But these passages refer not to the Ethiopic but to the Slavonic Enoch. In the first passage the italicized words *all the highest storehouses* refer to Paradise and hell which are described in viii, ix–x of the Slavonic Enoch. Moreover the next italicized words, *the tree of life in the middle of the garden*, are an actual quotation from viii. 3 of the same book. This tree is in Paradise according to *Slavonic Enoch* viii. 3 but in the neighbourhood of the chief of the seven great mountains according to the *Ethiopic Enoch* xxiv. 3–xxv. In the second passage the reference of *the storehouses of the upper and lower kingdoms* to *Slavonic Enoch* viii–x is still clearer than in the first: similarly the words *tree of life* are derived from the same source. On the other hand what are we to make of the phrase *the tree concerning which Adam received the commandment*? It may refer to *Ethiopic Enoch* xxxvi. 3–6 since there is no mention of this tree in the *Slavonic Enoch*. But the conjunction of these two trees in the Zohar does not necessarily imply that they were represented as together in the Paradise of Adam. If the words *the tree concerning which Adam received the commandment* refer at all to the *Ethiopic Enoch* they are sufficiently explained by xxxii. 3–6. We have already shown that the phrase *tree of life in the middle of the garden* is from *Slavonic Enoch* viii. 3.

The error may have started in the Greek source. The text reads *notos* (south wind) which may be a corruption of *notis* or *notia* meaning **moisture.** Or **south** may have been a marginal note explaining **from there.** Thus *q* omits it along with the following **and.** The fact that *tu, abcklx,* and the α group omit this **and** even though they include **south** may support this. *u* resolves the problem by reading **from the south, dew** instead of **from there, south and dew.** <gloss>26</gloss> Manuscripts *abc* omit. <gloss>27</gloss> Manuscript *m* omits.

## XXXVIII. The First Parable

->When the congregation of the righteous shall appear,<-
->And sinners are judged for their sins,<-
->And are driven from the face of the dry ground;<-

->2. And when the Righteous One shall appear before the eyes of the righteous,<-
->Whose chosen works are hung upon the Lord of Spirits,<-
->And light shall appear to the righteous and the chosen who dwell upon the dry ground,<-
->Where then will be the dwelling of the sinners,<-
->And where the resting-place of those who have denied the Lord of Spirits?<-
->It would have been better for them if they had never been born.<-

->3. When the secrets of the righteous shall be revealed,<-
->The sinners shall be judged,<-
->And the godless driven from the presence of the righteous and the chosen.<-

->4. And from that time on, those who possess the earth shall no longer be powerful and exalted,<-
->Nor shall they be able to behold the face of the holy,<-
->For the Lord of Spirits has caused His light to appear on the face of the holy, the righteous, and the chosen.<-

# The Book of Enoch: XXXVIII. 5—XXXIX. 5.

5. 6. And from then on, there shall be no one to intercede for them with the **Lord of Spirits** <note>original: "እግዚአ፡ መንፈሳት" (Egzi'a Menfesat) — a primary title for God in the Book of Enoch</note> [because their life is at an end.

### Chapter XXXIX
1. And it shall come to pass in those days that the children of the **chosen and holy** <note>referring to the righteous elect or perhaps the angelic "Watchers" who remained faithful</note> shall descend from the high heavens, and their seed shall become one with the children of men. 2. 3. And in those days a whirlwind <note>original: "ዐውሎ፡ ነፋት" — a storm wind or tempest</note> snatched me up from the face of the earth, and set me down at the **edge of the heavens**. <note>original: "ጽንፈ፡ ሰማያት" — the boundary or extremity of the celestial realms</note>

4. And there I saw another vision: the dwelling places of the holy, and the resting places of the righteous.

5. There my eyes saw their dwellings with the **angels of righteousness** <note>original: "መላእክተ፡ ጽድቅ"</note>, and their resting places with the holy ones; and they were petitioning and making supplication and praying on behalf of the children of men; and **righteousness** flowed like water before them, and mercy like dew upon the earth.

# THE BOOK OF ENOCH XXXIX. 10—XL. 4.

And I blessed Him, saying: "Blessed is He, and may He be blessed from the beginning <note>original: *em-qedme*; can also mean 'from before the world'</note> and forevermore."

### XL.
And after this I saw thousands of thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand—they were beyond number or reckoning—who stand before the Lord of Spirits. 2. # XLIV. 1 — XLV. 5. The Book of Enoch

### Chapter XLV
1. And this is the second parable <note>The "Parables" are the second major section of the Book of Enoch, focusing on the coming Judgment and the Messiah.</note> concerning those who deny the name of the dwelling of the holy ones and the Lord of Spirits. <note>original: "Egzi'a Manfasat" — a primary title for God in this text, often translated as Lord of Spirits.</note>

2. They shall not ascend into heaven,
And on the earth they shall not come;
Such shall be the lot of the sinners who have denied the name of the Lord of Spirits,

And he shall test <note>original: "yahari" — the translator notes a likely corruption from a root meaning 'to choose' to one meaning 'to test' or 'examine' based on Aramaic/Greek parallels.</note> their deeds,
And their resting places shall be without number.
And their spirit shall grow strong within them
When they see my Chosen Ones,
And those who have appealed to my glorious name.

4. On that day, I will cause my Chosen One to dwell among them,
And I will transform the heaven and make it a blessing and a light forever.

5. And I will transform the earth and make it a blessing;
And I will cause my chosen ones to dwell upon it,
But those who commit sin and wrongdoing shall not set foot upon it.

---

and "they raise" does not. Compare Ecclesiasticus 10:14: "The Lord has cast down the thrones of proud princes"; Wisdom of Solomon 5:23: "and shall turn upside down the thrones of the mighty." Now we can with some certainty determine the Hebrew lying behind "He shall cast down" <note>original: ይገሬትሕ (yegereth)</note>; for in the next verse (46:6a) we find this verb recurs in the phrase "He shall cast down the faces," which equals the Hebrew phrase *yappil panim* <note>original: יפיל פנים - literally "to make the face fall"</note> (see 48:8 for the passive construction). Thus "He shall cast down the kings from their thrones and from their kingdoms" equals the Hebrew: *wayyappil et-hammelakim mikesotam umimmamlakotam* <note>original: ויפיל את־המלכים מכסאותיהם וממመልכותיהם</note>. This verse was probably written in the margin as a more correct form of 46:4a. "They raise" then in our text equals the Greek *exairei* <note>original: ἐξαιρεῖ - takes away</note> or *anoisei* <note>original: ἀνοίσει - shall carry up</note> which equals the Hebrew *yitol* <note>original: יטול</note> corrupt for *yappil* <note>original: יפיל</note>. Hence for "raise" read "He shall cast them down." The above conclusions postulate the existence not only of a Hebrew text, but also of a manuscript with marginal alternative readings. $^1$ Manuscript $u$ omits. "He loosened the sinners" is a strange phrase. $^2$ Manuscript $q$ reads "for the heat." $^3$ Equals "He shall break the teeth" <note>original: συνትρίψει τοὺς ὀδόντας</note> from Psalms 3:8; 58:6. $^4$ Manuscripts $qu, \beta.$ $g m$ read "their thrones upon their thrones." $t$ "from their thrones upon their thrones." $^5$ $g m.$ $q t u, \beta$ read "their kingdom." $^6$ Manuscript $c$ omits. $^7$ $g t u, \beta.$ $m q$ read "they exalt him." $^8$ $m t u, \beta.$ $g$ reads "he praises," $q$ "they praise." $^9$ $a x$ add "to him." $^{10}$ $g$ adds "that is." $^{11}$ Compare Wisdom of Solomon 6:3: "For power is given you from the Lord" <note>original: ἐδόθη παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡ κράτησις ὑμῖν</note>. $^{12}$ Manuscript $d$ prefixes "and." $^{13}$ $a, e h o (v w) b. a b c d f k l n x, a$ read "shame." # The Book of Enoch: XLVI. 7—XLVII. 1.

->And$^1$ they lift up their hands$^2$ toward the Most High,<-
->And they tread upon$^4$ the dry ground and$^3$ dwell$^5$ therein,<-
->And$^6$ all their deeds manifest unrighteousness,$^7$<-
->And their power rests upon their riches,<-
->And their faith is in the gods$^9$ which they have made with their hands,<-
->And they deny$^{10}$ the name$^{11}$ of the Lord of Spirits.$^{12}$<-
->8. And they are driven forth$^{13}$ from the houses of his congregations,$^{15}$<-
->And the$^{16}$ faithful who hang upon the name of the Lord of Spirits.$^{12}$<-
->XLVII. And in those days the prayer$^{18}$ of the righteous ascended.$^{17}$<-

<note>The following section is a technical commentary by the editor, R.H. Charles, regarding the reconstruction of the original text.</note>

There is an intrusion of verse $7^b$ between $7^a$ and $7^c$. If $7^b$ is genuine, it came immediately after "They are those who..." Turning now to $7^c$, we see that it is senseless as it stands. "And they tread upon the dry ground" <note>original Ge'ez: ወይከይዱ፡ ዲበ፡ የብስ፡</note> = "and they trample upon the earth" <note>original Greek: καὶ καταπατοῦσιν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν</note>. We have only to supply an accusative <note>a direct object</note> to the verb here, i.e., read "they tread them down" <note>original Ge'ez: ይከይድዎሙ፡</note> = "they trample them" <note>original Greek: καταπατοῦσιν αὐτούς</note> in order to bring the text into line with Daniel 8:10, save that the latter connects the "upon the earth" with the preceding clause. It is now obvious that "and dwell therein" is a senseless addition. Moreover, this phrase, which has here a bad ethical sense, always has good ethical associations throughout the genuine sections of the Similitudes <note>The "Similitudes" is a specific section of 1 Enoch (chapters 37–71) featuring parables about the Son of Man</note>. Cf. 37:2; 40:6, 7; 48:5. In the interpolations <note>later additions not part of the original text</note>, however, it carries with it doubtful or bad associations: cf. 54:9; 55:1; 60:5; 65:6, etc. Returning now to $7^a$, the verb in this clause = "they judge" <note>original Hebrew: ידינו</note> which seems corrupt for "they cast down" <note>original Hebrew: יפילו</note> = "they cast down" <note>original Greek: καταβάλλουσι</note>. For "they lift up" <note>original Ge'ez: ይሌዕሉ፡</note> we should then read "they cast down" <note>original Ge'ez: ይወርዱ፡</note>. The stanza should then be read as follows:—

->And they are those who$^1$ lift up their hands toward the Most High,<-
->And$^{7^d}$ they cast down the stars of heaven,<-
->And they tread them down upon the dry ground.<-

Since the stanzas before and after consist of distichs <note>two-line units of verse</note>, it is possible that the words "lift up their hands toward the Most High and" are an interpolation. $^1$ manuscript $q$ omits. $^2$ manuscripts $g, \beta$. $m, q, t, u$ read "their hand." $^3$ $q$ omits; possibly $u$ originally. $^4$ $m$ reads "into"; $c$ omits. $^5$ $g, t^1$ read "they dwelt." $^6$ $m$ reads "all." $^7$ manuscripts $a-q, d, e, f, h, k, l, y, a$. $q, b$ omit. $t^2, a, b, c, o, x$ read "and they manifest." All manuscripts but $q, u, en, b$ make a double-writing error here. $g, m$ add "and all their deeds are unrighteousness." $t, a, b, c, d, f, h, k, l, o, x, a$ add "deeds of unrighteousness." $^8$ $g, m$ omit. $^9$ $t^1, u$ read "to the god." $^{10}$ $a-q, l, a$. $q, e, f, h, k, o, p (v, w), b$ read "they deny." $a, b, c, x$ "they denied him." $n$ "they denied." $^{11}$ $m, t, u, b, c, d, l, a$. $g$ omits. $q, e, f, h, k, n, o, p (v, w)$ read "the name" for "his name." $^{12}$ $g, m$. Other manuscripts read "spirits." $^{13}$ $g, t$. $m, q, u, \beta$ read "and they are driven forth." $^{14}$ $g, m, t^1, u$. $q, t^2, \beta$ read "from the houses." $^{15}$ $g, q, u$ (save that $q$ writes last letter as 'e'). $m$ reads "assembly." $t, d, e, f, h, k, l, o, a, b, p$ "houses of congregation." $a, b, x$ "place of assembly." $c$ "houses of congregation." $^{16}$ $t^1$ reads "for." $a, b, x$ "and." $^{17}$ $u, a, b, c, d, e$. $g$ reads "ascent." $m, t, f, h, k, l, n, o, x, a, b$ "it ascended." $q$ "he ascended." $^{18}$ $a, x$ add "of the holy ones."

### The Book of Enoch

1. And the *blood* <note>original: "demu"</note> of the righteous <note>The plural "righteous ones" is used here, referring to the martyrs.</note> ascended from the earth before the Lord of Spirits. <note>original: "Egzi'a Menfesat" — a primary title for God in this section of Enoch.</note>

2. In those days, the holy ones who dwell in the heights of heaven shall unite with one voice; they shall petition, pray, laud, give thanks, and bless the name of the Lord of Spirits on behalf of the blood of the righteous which has been shed. They pray that the prayer of the righteous may not be in vain <note>literally: "may not cease" or "not be silent"</note> before the Lord of Spirits, so that judgment <note>term: "zhe" — justice or a legal decision</note> may be executed for them, and that their patience <note>or "endurance"</note> might not have to last forever.

3. In those days, I saw the Head of Days <note>A title for God, often translated as the "Ancient of Days," representing eternal existence.</note> as He sat upon the throne of His glory; and the books of the living <note>The heavenly ledgers recording the deeds and names of the faithful.</note> were opened before Him, and all His host which is in the heights of heaven and His attendants stood before Him.

4. And the hearts of the holy ones were filled with joy, because the number <note>The "full number" or "tally" of the martyrs required before the end times.</note> of the righteous had been offered, <note>The text suggests the count is being fulfilled or drawn near.</note> and the prayer of the righteous had been heard, and the blood of the righteous was required <note>meaning "accounted for" or "avenged"</note> before the Lord of Spirits.

# LVIII. 5—LX. 2. THE BOOK OF ENOCH

...that they should seek the secrets of righteousness, the portion of faith;

### LIX.

and they flash for a blessing or for a curse, as the Lord of Spirits wills. 2. And there I saw

and the †dwellings <note>The translator notes a likely corruption in the original Greek source: the word for "dwellings" (oikēmata) was likely mistaken for "judgments" (krimata).</note> of the dry land appeared, [and the voice of the thunder] for peace and for blessing, or
for a curse, according to the word of the Lord of Spirits. 3. And after that, all the
secrets of the lights and of the lightnings were shown to me; and they flash for blessing and for satisfaction.

# LXIII. 2-6. The Book of Enoch 115

->The Book of Enoch<-

\*Blessed is He, the Lord of Spirits,¹ \*and your Lord of Kings,²
\*and your Lord of the Mighty,⁴ and your Lord of the Rich,⁶
and the Lord of Glory, and the Lord of Wisdom.

3. And Your power reveals⁸ all hidden things¹¹ to all generations,
and Your glory is for ever and ever.¹³
Deep are all¹⁴ Your secrets which cannot be numbered,¹⁷
and Your righteousness is beyond calculation.¹⁹

4. Now we have learned that \*we should glorify and bless²⁰ the Lord of Kings,²³
and Him who reigns over all kings.

5. And they shall say:²⁴ "Who would grant us²⁵ rest so that²⁷ \*we might glorify and give thanks²⁸
and make our confession before His glory?"²⁹

6. And now³⁰ we beg for rest, we seek it and find it not;³¹
\*we are driven away³² and do not possess it;³³
and light has passed away from before us,
and darkness is our dwelling-place³⁶ for ever and ever.³⁷

For man was not *created* <note>original: "ኢተፈጥረ" (i-tafatra)</note> otherwise than as the angels, that they should remain *righteous and pure*, and death, which destroys everything, would not have touched them; but through this knowledge of theirs they are perishing, and through this power <note>The "power" of forbidden knowledge or the "power" of death.</note> it <note>The text here is difficult; the translator suggests it may mean "it devours me" or "they are devoured."</note> devours me.

12. And the *fifth* is named Kasdeyal: this is *he* who showed the children of men all the wicked smitings of spirits and demons, and the smitings of the *embryo in the womb* <note>original: "ዓዛባል፡ ማሕፀን" (azabal mahtsan) - referring to abortions or injuries to the unborn.</note> so that it passes away, and [the smiting of the soul], the bites of the serpent, and the smiting which happens at noon <note>A reference to the "Noonday Demon" mentioned in Psalm 91:6.</note>, the son of the serpent named Taba'et.

13. This is the number <note>The translator notes that the Ge'ez word for "number" (ጐልቈ) likely translates a Hebrew term meaning "task" or "charge."</note> of *Kasbeel*, the head of the oath, who showed [the oath] to the holy ones when he dwelt on high in *glory*, and its name is Beqa.

4. And he showed me all the secrets of the ends <margin>1. One manuscript omits "ends."</margin> of heaven, and all the treasuries of the stars and the luminaries, from where <margin>4. One manuscript reads "who."</margin> they go out before the face of the holy ones.

5. And my spirit was hidden <insert>and Enoch</insert> <note>The name "Enoch" is likely a later addition by a scribe to clarify who is being hidden; various manuscripts insert it differently, such as "Enoch said" or "that Enoch."</note> into the heaven of heavens, and I saw there <insert>in the midst of that light</insert> <note>This phrase is likely a gloss explaining the word "there."</note> something built of crystals <term>crystals: literally "hailstones" or "ice-stones," often used in ancient texts to describe dazzling, transparent heavenly material</term>, and in the midst of those stones were tongues of living fire.

6. And my spirit saw a circuit <note>The original Ge'ez suffix here acts like a definite article: "the circuit."</note> which surrounded that house of fire, and on its four sides were rivers full of living fire, and they surrounded that house.

7. And around it were the Seraphim, the Cherubim, and the Ophannin <term>Ophannin: literally "the Wheels," a high order of angels described in Ezekiel's vision</term>; these are they who do not sleep and who guard the throne of the glory of God.

8. And I saw angels who could not be numbered, thousands of thousands and ten thousand times ten thousands, surrounding that house; and Michael, Raphael, Gabriel, and Phanuel, and the holy angels who are above in the heavens, go in and out of that house.

***

# The Book of Enoch LXXI. 9-13.

9. And there came forth from that house
Michael and Raphael and Gabriel and Phanuel,
and many holy angels without number.
10. And with them was the Head of Days <note>original: "Re'ese Mawā'el" — a title for God the Father, often translated as the "Ancient of Days"</note>,
and His head was like white wool, pure and clean,
and His raiment was indescribable.
11. And I fell upon my face,
and all my flesh melted,
and my spirit was transformed;
and I cried out with a loud voice . . . <note>The ellipsis indicates a likely corruption or gap in the original manuscript tradition.</note>
in the spirit of power,
and I blessed and glorified and exalted.
12. And those blessings which went forth from my mouth were well-pleasing before that
Head of Days. 13. And that Head of Days came with Michael and Raphael
and Gabriel and Phanuel, and tens of thousands and myriads <term>myriad: a unit of ten thousand; used here to denote an infinite multitude</term> of angels without number.

14. And he came to me <note>original: "ውእቱ" (he/that one)</note> and with his voice he greeted me and said to me:
"You are the Son of Man <note>The Ethiopic "ወልደ፡ ብእሲ" (Son of Man) here identifies Enoch himself with the messianic figure seen in previous visions.</note>

and the righteousness of the Head of Days shall not forsake you."

and so it shall be unto you for ever and ever."

16. And all shall walk in your path, since righteousness never forsakes you;
with you shall be their dwelling place, and with you their portion,
and from you they shall not be separated for ever and ever.

and peace shall be for the righteous, and a straight path <note>original: "ፍኖተ፡ ርትዕ" (path of uprightness)</note> for the righteous,
in the name of the Lord of Spirits for ever and ever.

### LXXII. The Book of the Courses of the Luminaries of Heaven: how it is with each one of them,
according to their classes, according to their dominion and their seasons, according to their names and their places of origin, and according to their months, which Uriel, the holy angel who was with me, who is their guide, showed to me; and he showed me all their laws exactly as they are, and how it is with regard to all the years of the world until eternity, until a new creation <note>original: "ግብረ፡ ኃይል" (deed of power/new creation)</note> is made which shall endure for ever.

# The Book of Enoch LXXII. 2-7.

2. And this is the first law of the luminaries: the light of the sun has its rising in the gates of heaven which are toward the east, and its setting in the gates of heaven which are toward the west. 3. And I saw six gates from which the sun rises, and six gates where the sun sets; and the moon rises and sets in these gates, as do the leaders of the stars with those whom they lead: six in the east and six in the west <note>The text describes a symmetrical cosmology where the sun, moon, and stars share specific portals in the sky.</note>. All of them follow one another in order, and there are many window-openings <term>maskot: windows or apertures</term> to the right and to the left of those gates. 4. And first there goes forth the great luminary whose name is the Sun, and its circumference is like the circumference of heaven, and it is quite full of illuminating and heating fire. 5. The chariot <note>original: "seregelat"</note> on which it ascends is driven by the wind, and the sun sets from the heaven and returns through the north <note>The text implies a circular path where the sun travels back to the east behind the scenes during the night.</note> in order to reach the east, and is guided so that it enters that gate and shines on the face of heaven. 6. In this way it rises in the first month in the great gate, [it rises] which is the fourth [of those six gates which are toward the east of the sun]. 7. And in that fourth gate from which the sun rises in the first month, there are twelve window-openings from which a flame goes forth when they are opened in their appropriate seasons.

8. When the sun sets <note>original: "ፀሐይ"</note> from the heaven, it departs through that third gate <note>original: "ኆኅት ሣልስ"</note> of the east, and in the fourth gate, which is in the west of heaven, it descends directly. 9. ### Critical Notes
<margin>1. *q* omits next five words through homoeoteleuton <note>A scribal error where the eye skips from one word to a similar one later in the text.</note>.</margin>
<margin>2. *t², β*. *a* has preserved the word but in the wrong context... *t²β* here represent the older text by preserving "moon" in its right context.</margin>
<margin>3. Emended from "from the sun" of *g m t*. *q u, t²β* omit. The sun and stars are the subject of "bring in"; this construction can stand though a plural verb would be more usual.</margin>
<margin>4. *u. g m t* read "and from the stars." *t², β* omit. After "and stars" all manuscripts except *n* add "and moon." Our author advocates a solar and sidereal year as the author of the *Book of Jubilees*, vi. 32-36. The unemended text which represents the moon as the perfect time divider is in glaring contradiction with verses 10, 11 and with *Jubilees*.</margin>
<margin>5. *m, β*. *g* reads "for the year." *q t u* "for the years."</margin>
<margin>6. *t. g m q* read "exactly" (feminine). *u, t²β* "exactly" (plural).</margin>
<margin>13. *g* omits. *m* reads "exactly." But probably "exactly" and "in justice" are alternative renderings of the Greek *en aletheia* <note>original: "ἐν ἀληθείᾳ" meaning "in truth" or "truly".</note>.</margin>
<margin>15. *q t* read "three hundred and sixty and four days."</margin>
<margin>18. *t* reads "ten hundred and eighty hundred and ninety." <note>Ethiopic numerals can be complex; the translator is noting variations in how the scribes wrote out the numbers 1,092.</note></margin>
<margin>25. *g u, β. t* writes in full "ten and nineteen hundred." In *q* both numerals are erased.</margin>

# The Book of Enoch LXXXII. 14-18.

Those who lead them are Adnarel, <note>original: "አድናርኤል"</note> and Iasusuel, and Ielomeel; these three follow behind the **leaders of the orders**, and <insert>they do not fail</insert> behind the leaders of the orders. These follow behind the leaders of the stations, <note>The "stations" refer to the fixed positions of the stars or the points of the zodiac.</note> who divide the four parts of the year.

15. At the beginning of the year, the first <term>rises</term> <note>The term "rises" (yaserq) refers to the heliacal rising of a star or the sun.</note> and rules with him whom he has named **Tam'ani** <note>original: "ተመአኒ"; likely derived from the Hebrew word for "Southern."</note> and the **sun**, and **all** the days of his authority, which they rule, are ninety-one days.

16. And these are the signs of the days which are to appear upon the earth in the **days** of his authority: sweat, and **heat**, and anxiety; <note>The Ge'ez "zehaz" is difficult to translate; it often implies distress or parching heat.</note> and **all** the trees bear fruit, and leaves come forth on all the trees; and the harvest of wheat, and the rose-flower, and **all the flowers** which come forth in the field; but the trees of winter wither.

17. And these are the names of their leaders who are under them: Barkiel, <note>original: "ብርክኤል"; likely "Blessing of God."</note> Zelbelsael, and another who is added as a head of a thousand, named Heloyaseph; and the days of the authority of this one are completed.

18. The other leader who is behind him is Heleemmelek, whom they call the name of the **Sun**.

## Book of Enoch

to the heaven, and how the sun <note>original: "ፀሐይ" (ṣeḥay)</note> comes out from the east, and the moon descends in the west, and the few stars, and all the earth, and everything that He has known <note>The translator notes a potential corruption in the original Greek or Hebrew source here regarding the word "known" versus "made."</note> from the beginning. ¹ *mt, β-n. g q* read **all** <note>original: ኵሎ፡</note> *u* omits. ² *gu. m q t, β* read **footstool** <note>original: መከያደ፡</note> ³ *n* omits.
⁴ *mu* omit. ⁵ *n* reads **you created** <note>original: ፈጠርከ፡</note> *e h k n* add **everything.** ⁶ *g m q. t* transposes after **you rule.** *u* omits. *β-ehn* read **everything.** *n* reads **everything** and transposes after **you.** *e h* omit. ⁷ *d l o y a, b* read **you fill.** *u* adds **to you.** ⁸ *a-g, β-d f n o p. g* reads **everything strengthens you.** *d f* **does not strengthen you.** *o, β* **strengthens you.** ⁹ *q* reads **deed.** ¹⁰ *g u, β-h i. m t, h i* read **and one.** *q* **and one.** ¹¹ *u* reads **and.** *x* **and one.** I have bracketed this phrase as a <term>dittography</term> <note>A scribal error where a letter or word is accidentally repeated.</note>. The repeated text appearing first as **and 10 and 10** was next expanded into **and 10 and one** as in *g, β-h i*, in order to bring the repetition into grammatical agreement with **Wisdom** or into **and one and one** of *q m t, h i*. But the repetition cannot be connected with **Wisdom**, for ‘wisdom’ is here personified as the subsequent clauses show. ¹² Emended. *g* reads **you...** *n* **you do not pass away.** Other manuscripts: **you do not pass away.** ¹³ Emended from **and it does not turn away** (**and it does not turn you** *g q* **and you do not turn** *m*) **from the state** (*q u* omit) **of your throne** (**your throne** *g* **from your throne** *m q*) (+ **forever** *n*) **and.** By this simple transposition of the verb **it does not turn away**, the parallelism of the text is restored. Further, **from the state** has been emended into **from the station.** Thus the phrase **from the station of your throne** = *from the place of your throne* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ τόπου τοῦ θρόνου σου</note> = *from the foundation of your dwelling* <note>original Hebrew: מִמְּכוֹן שִׁבְתְּךָ</note> Psalm 89:14. To return now to the word **from the state**, which I have emended into **from the station**, we should observe that it does not admit of any reasonable rendering in this passage. The word means ‘state,’ ‘condition,’ ‘life,’ or ‘food.’ Even if we forced upon it the meaning of *basis of life*, as Flemming has done, the sense is not suitable to the passage. ¹⁴ *e i v* transpose after **you know.** *u* omits. ¹⁵ *t u. g* reads **you know and.** *m, β* **you know and.** *q* omits. ¹⁶ *g* adds **and you appear.** ¹⁷ *t, β.* *a-t* read **that which was hidden.** ¹⁸ Bracketed as a <term>gloss</term> <note>An explanatory note added by a later scribe that worked its way into the main text.</note>. ¹⁹ *u* reads **your angels.** ²⁰ *u* omits. ²¹ *m* omits. ²² *q.* Other manuscripts read **day.** ²³ *g.* Other manuscripts omit. ²⁴ *u* omits. *n* transposes after next word. ²⁵ *t u, β-e. g m q, e* omit. ²⁶ *u, e* omit.

# The Book of Enoch: LXXXIX. 5-10.

5. 7. And that white bull passed away from them. <note>The three bulls represent the sons of Noah: Shem (white), Ham (black), and Japheth (red/ruddy). The "passing away" refers to Noah's death.</note>

# The Book of Enoch: LXXXIX. 10-15.

10. ...and wild boars <note>original: "ሐሬዊያ ገዳም" (ḥarewiya gadām) — standard interpretations suggest these are the various non-Israelite nations</note>, and foxes, and hyenas, and wild boars, and night-ravens, and leopards, and monkeys, and wild dogs, and ravens; and there was born among them a **white bull**. <note>The "white bull" here refers to Abraham.</note>

11. And they began to bite one another, but that white bull which was born among them begat a wild ass and a white bull with him <note>representing Ishmael (the wild ass) and Isaac (the white bull)</note>, and the wild asses multiplied.

12. And that bull <note>Isaac</note> which was born from him begat a **black wild boar** <note>representing Esau, the ancestor of the Edomites</note> and a **white sheep** <note>representing Jacob, the ancestor of the Israelites</note>; and that boar begat many boars, and that sheep begat twelve sheep. <note>The twelve sons of Jacob, the progenitors of the Twelve Tribes of Israel.</note>

13. And when those twelve sheep had grown up, they handed over one of their own <note>Joseph</note> to the [wild] asses <note>The Midianites/Ishmaelites who purchased Joseph</note>, and those asses in turn handed over that sheep to the **wolves** <note>The Egyptians</note>; and that sheep grew up among the wolves.

14. And the Lord brought the twelve sheep so that they might dwell with him and pasture with him among the wolves, and they multiplied and became many flocks of sheep. <note>This refers to the migration of Jacob's family to Egypt during the famine and their subsequent growth as a people.</note>

15. And the wolves began to fear them, and they oppressed them until they began to destroy their children, and they cast their children into much water <note>The Nile River, where Pharaoh ordered Hebrew male infants to be drowned</note>; and those sheep began to cry out because of their children.

# The Book of Enoch: LXXXIX. 15-24.

15. And they cried <note>original: "ይስክዩ" (yiskeyu) — to cry out in distress or appeal for help</note> to their Lord. 

16. And the sheep <note>Moses</note> who had been saved from the dogs <note>The Egyptians; while earlier called "wolves," the text here uses "dogs" ('aklabāt) to describe the oppressors</note> fled and dwelt in a desert enclosure. And I saw the sheep as they wandered and were troubled, and they begged their Lord with all their strength until that **Lord of the Sheep** descended from His high palace <note>original: "ጽርሐ" (ṣerḥa) — a lofty hall or celestial dwelling</note> to the voice of the sheep, and He came to them and looked upon them. 

17. And He called that sheep which had risen up from the dogs, and spoke to him concerning the dogs, that they should listen to him and <note>original: "ከመ ኢይግስስዎሙ" (kama iyigseswomu)</note> touch the sheep no more. 

18. And the sheep went to the dogs by the word of the Lord, and another sheep <note>Aaron</note> was found and went with him, and they both went together into the assembly of those dogs; and he spoke with them and warned them that from that time forth they should not touch the sheep. 

19. And then I saw the dogs, how their mouths grew exceedingly strong against the sheep with all their power, and the sheep cried out. 

20. And their Lord came to the sheep and began to strike those dogs, and the dogs began to wail <note>original: "የአውዱ" (ya'awdu) — can mean to circle or to lament loudly</note>, but the sheep remained silent and did not cry out from that moment. 

21. And I saw the sheep until they departed from the dogs; and the eyes of the dogs were darkened, and they went out following the sheep with all their power. 

22. And the Lord of the Sheep went with them, leading them, and all His sheep followed Him; and His face was glorious and honorable and terrible to behold. 

23. And the dogs began to pursue all those sheep until they reached them at a certain pool of water <note>The Red Sea</note>. 

24. And that pool of water was divided <note>original: "ተሠጠ" (taśaṭa) — split or rent asunder</note>, and the water stood on this side and on that side before their faces.

# LXXXIX. 37-41.
## The Book of Enoch

<margin>37.</margin> And I saw until that sheep—the one that had been found <note>This refers to Moses, who "was found" in the bulrushes and led the people.</note> and had led them—fell asleep <note>In this symbolic vision, "falling asleep" represents death.</note>; and I saw until all the sheep perished, both great and small. Then others arose in their place and they came into a pasture, and they approached a stream of water <note>The Jordan River, marking the boundary of the Promised Land.</note>.

<margin>38.</margin> And that sheep which led them, **which had become a man**, was separated from them and fell asleep; and all the sheep sought him and cried out over him with a great crying. <note>This depicts the mourning of the Israelites after the death of Moses.</note>

<margin>39.</margin> And I saw until they were silent from their crying for that sheep; and they crossed that stream of water. And there stood the two sheep <note>Scholars identify these two as Joshua and Caleb, the only leaders of the original generation allowed to enter the land.</note> who led them in the place of those who had fallen asleep and had led them before.

<margin>40.</margin> And I saw the sheep until they entered a **goodly place** and a **pleasant and glorious land**; and I saw those sheep until they were satisfied; and that house <note>The Tabernacle, the portable sanctuary of the Israelites.</note> was in their midst in the pleasant land.

<margin>41.</margin> And sometimes their eyes were opened, and sometimes they were blinded <note>This refers to the cyclical nature of the Book of Judges: the people would "be blinded" (fall into idolatry), suffer, and then their eyes would "be opened" (repent) when a leader was sent.</note>, until another sheep <note>Likely the prophet Samuel, who transitioned the nation toward the monarchy.</note> arose and led them and brought them all back, and their eyes were opened.

### Critical Notes
<note>The following notes refer to variations found in the original Ethiopic manuscripts (labeled with letters like g, m, q) and comparisons with early Greek fragments.</note>

1. Manuscripts *g, m,* and *q* include this. *tu* and others read "and wild boars."
2. Manuscript *a* reads "those," while others read "these."
3. Manuscript *n* reads "and."
4. Manuscripts *g* and *n* match the Greek word for "raised up" <note>original: "ἤγειρεν"</note>. Other manuscripts are corrupted, likely because of an error in the grammar of the following addition.
5. Manuscript *n* reads "for them."
6. Several manuscripts omit "Lord of the sheep"—an attempt to fix the text after it became corrupted in earlier copies.
16. The Greek text gives "the sheep" <note>original: "τὰ πρόβατα"</note> in the plural, referring to the faithful Israelites. This is likely the original meaning. In the singular, it would refer to Samuel, though Samuel is called a "lamb" <note>original: "ἀμνός"</note> in the next verse.
17. I have added "who" <note>original: "ዘ" (za)</note> before the word for "opened" to match the Greek. In the uncorrected Ethiopic, the sheep was the subject of the opening, but the grammar for "eyes being opened" usually requires the eyes to be the subject.
25. The Greek fragment reads "this lamb" <note>original: "τὸν ἄρνα τοῦτον"</note>.
30. Manuscript *d* is the source here; other manuscripts just say "sheep."
37. Manuscript *m* reads "in all that," while *n* reads "in all this."

> <gloss>1</gloss> The Ethiopic text adds: "and that ram begat many sheep, and he fell asleep; and a small sheep became a ram in his stead, and became the ruler and leader of those sheep." <note>This likely refers to the transition from King David to King Solomon. ### LXXXIX. 72—XC. 1. The Book of Enoch

...who fell from that house; and the **wild boars of the field** <note>original: "ሐራውያ፡ ገዳም" (ḥarāwyā gadām). In this allegory, the wild boars usually represent the Edomites, enemies of the returning exiles.</note> began to help them. 73. And they began again to build as before, and they raised up that **tower**, and it was called the **high tower**; <note>The "tower" symbolizes the Temple in Jerusalem. The "high tower" refers to the Second Temple, rebuilt after the Babylonian exile.</note> and they began again to place a table before the tower, but **all the bread** upon it was **polluted and not pure**. <note>The author of Enoch, likely writing from a sectarian perspective, views the Second Temple's offerings as illegitimate or "unclean" (original: "ርኩስ", rekus).</note> 74. And as for all those sheep, their eyes were blinded so that they could not see, and their shepherds likewise; and they delivered them to their shepherds for destruction, and they trampled the sheep with their feet and devoured them. 75. And the Lord of the Sheep remained silent until all the sheep were scattered over the field and mixed with the beasts, and He did not save them from the hand of the beasts. 76. And he who wrote the book <note>The heavenly scribe, often identified as Enoch himself or the archangel Michael, recording the crimes of the seventy shepherds.</note> ascended, and showed it, and read it before the Lord of the Sheep, and he petitioned Him on their behalf, and besought Him on their behalf as he showed Him all the deeds of the shepherds, and gave evidence before Him against all the shepherds. 77. And he took that book and deposited it with Him, and departed.

# XC.

1. And I saw until the time that **seventy-seven** <note>The Ge'ez text here says 77 (፸ወ፯), though various manuscripts vary between 70, 75, or 80. These represent the successive angelic administrations of the world.</note> shepherds had pastured [the sheep] in this manner, and they completed [their periods].

# The Book of Enoch

All of them in their own time, **as the first ones** <note>original: "ቀዳማውያን" (qadāmāwyān). This refers to the previous groups of shepherds who presided over the flock during the Exile.</note> and in their seasons, they received them into their hands so that they might pasture them in their seasons, every shepherd in his own time. **2.** And then I saw in **my vision all the birds of heaven arrived: eagles, and vultures, and kites, and ravens.** <note>These birds represent the foreign world powers: the eagles and vultures likely symbolize the Greeks and the Ptolemaic/Seleucid empires who dominated Judea.</note> The eagles led all the birds, and they began to devour those sheep, and they pecked out their eyes and ate their flesh. **3.** And the sheep cried out because their flesh was being devoured by the birds; and **I looked and lamented in my sleep over that shepherd who was pasturing the sheep.** <note>The visionary (Enoch) grieves because the angelic shepherd assigned to protect the flock is instead allowing the "birds" to destroy it.</note> **4.** And **I saw until those sheep were devoured by the dogs,** <note>The "dogs" likely represent the Philistines or other neighboring enemies.</note> **and by the eagles, and by the kites, and they left them no flesh, nor skin, nor sinew, until only their bones stood there; and their bones** fell upon the earth, and the sheep became few. **5.** And I saw until the time that twenty-seven shepherds had pastured [them], and they completed in their periods fifty-eight times. <note>These numbers are part of a complex chronological scheme in the Animal Apocalypse. The "seventy shepherds" are divided into groups; the 58 "times" represent the total number of shepherd-reigns passed by this point in the vision's history.</note> **6.** And **behold, lambs were born from those white sheep,** <note>The "white sheep" are the faithful of Israel. ## The Book of Enoch

**6.** ...they should open <note>original: "ይክሥቱ" (yekśetu); likely meaning to open their eyes or become aware.</note> and see, and cry out to the sheep. **7.** And they cried out to them, <note>Note 2: Manuscript variations suggest this could be "they called out" or "they shouted." <note>Translator's Note on the Critical Apparatus: The footnotes in the original text (indicated by numbers 1-35) track the differences between various Ethiopic manuscripts (labeled a, e, f, g, m, q, t, u, etc.). ### **Translator’s Notes on Textual Variations**
<note>The following notes explain differences found in the various ancient Ethiopian manuscripts used to reconstruct this text.</note>

*   **7.** Manuscript *d* reads "shall perish" instead of "shall increase." Manuscript *u* omits several words including "sin" and "great." Some manuscripts add "The Holy Lord shall come forth..." as a repetition.
*   **8.** Most manuscripts include the word "roots" (ሥራው), though manuscript *g* omits it.
*   **9.** Manuscript *u* omits the description of the fire. The word "temples" or "shameful things" (ማኅፈሪ) varies slightly in spelling across the documents.
*   **10.** Manuscript *m* emphasizes the singular "the righteous one," whereas others imply a collective rising of the righteous.
*   **11.** This entire verse is absent in some of the oldest versions, which is why it is marked with brackets.
*   **12.** There is significant variation in the word order for "Eighth Week" (ሳምንት ሰንበት); some manuscripts simply say "Sabbath" or "the Eighth."

## XCIII. And after this, Enoch gave to me <note>Some manuscripts read "Enoch began to speak" or "it happened that Enoch..."</note> and commanded me to speak from the books.

2. And Enoch spoke concerning the **children of righteousness**, and concerning the **elect of the world**, and concerning the **plant of uprightness** <note>original: 'ትክለ፡ ርትዕ' (təkla rətʿ) — a metaphor for the faithful people of God</note>;

10. Thus I say to you: He will not save you;
For He who created you will **cast you down**,
And upon your fall there shall be **no mercy**,
And your Creator will rejoice in your **destruction**. <note>The original Ge'ez term for "destruction" (<term>ሕጉለክሙ - hegulakomu</term>) implies a total loss or perishing. The image of the Creator rejoicing in the destruction of the wicked is a stark prophetic reversal of the usual mercy associated with the divine.</note>

11. And your righteous ones shall be, in those days, a **reproach**
To the sinners and the ungodly.

### XCV.
1. Who will give to my eyes <note>original: "Who will give me for my eyes..."</note> a cloud of water, 
That I might **weep** over you,
And pour out my tears like a rain cloud,
And find rest from the sorrow of my heart?

2. Who has allowed you to practice **hatred and evil**?
Judgment shall overtake you, O sinners!

3. **Fear not the sinners**, you righteous;
For the Lord will again deliver them into your hands,
That you may execute **judgment** upon them as you desire. <note>This "reversal of fortunes" is a common theme in apocalyptic literature; the persecuted righteous are promised a time when they will act as judges over their former oppressors.</note>

4. Woe to you who pronounce **anathemas** <note>The text refers to "binding oaths" or "curses" (<term>ግዘታተ - gezetata</term>) that were used as spiritual or legal weapons.</note> which cannot be undone;
**Healing** is far from you because of your sins.

5. Woe to you who repay your neighbor with **evil**;
For you shall be repaid according to your deeds.

# The Book of Enoch

6. Woe to you who are witnesses <gloss>2</gloss> of falsehood <gloss>3</gloss>
And to those who weigh <gloss>5</gloss> out iniquity,
For you shall suddenly perish. <gloss>6</gloss>

7. Woe to you, O sinners, because you persecute the righteous; <gloss>8</gloss>
For you shall be handed over <gloss>9</gloss> and **persecuted** <gloss>10</gloss> in **iniquity**,
And there shall **weigh heavy** <gloss>12</gloss> upon you <gloss>13</gloss> an evil yoke. <gloss>14</gloss> <note>The "evil yoke" refers to the spiritual and physical burden of judgment that the wicked will bear as a result of their oppression of others.</note>

XCVI. **Be hopeful** <gloss>15</gloss>, O **righteous**, for suddenly the sinners shall perish <gloss>16</gloss> from before you,
And **authority** <gloss>17</gloss> shall be yours <gloss>18</gloss> over them <gloss>19</gloss> just as <gloss>20</gloss> you desired.

2. And **on the day of the tribulation** of the sinners, your children shall be lifted up <gloss>22</gloss> and **raised** <gloss>23</gloss> like eagles;
**Your nest shall be higher than the vulture**, <gloss>24</gloss>
And more than the wood-pigeons <gloss>25</gloss> shall be your place of shelter; <gloss>26</gloss> <note>The text uses bird metaphors to describe safety and elevation. The righteous will find refuge in high, inaccessible places, far from the reach of the lawless.</note>
And you shall ascend and **enter** <gloss>27</gloss> into the clefts of the earth,
And into the crevices of the rock forever, like the one fleeing <gloss>28</gloss> from before the lawless; <gloss>29</gloss>
And they shall **groan** <gloss>31</gloss> over you and weep <gloss>32</gloss> like **sirens**. <gloss>33</gloss> <note>original: "ጼዴናት - tsedenat" refers to sirens or desert spirits; here it likely mimics the wailing sound of mourning.</note>

3. But as for you, do not fear, you who have suffered;
For <gloss>34</gloss> **healing** shall be yours, <gloss>35</gloss>
And a **bright light** <gloss>36</gloss> shall shine for you, <gloss>37</gloss>
And you shall hear **the voice of rest** <gloss>38</gloss> from heaven.

4. Woe to you, sinners! For your **wealth** makes you appear <note>The Ethiopic verb suggests a false or deceptive appearance of piety based on material success.</note> righteous, but your own hearts convict you, proving that you are indeed sinners. This very matter shall be a testimony against you, a **memorial of your evil deeds**.

5. Woe to you who eat the finest <note>Literally "the fat of the wheat," a common biblical idiom for the highest quality food.</note> wheat, and drink the strength of the deep spring <note>Scholars suggest the original Hebrew phrase meant "spiced wine," a luxury of the elite. Original: "hayla śerwa naq‘"</note>, and trample the humble with your power.

6. Woe to you who drink water at all times <note>The translator notes suggest this may be a corruption of "from every fountain," contrasting the physical water the rich consume with the spiritual fountain they neglect.</note>, for you shall be suddenly repaid; you shall fade and wither, because you have **forsaken the fountain of life**.

7. Woe to you who have committed unrighteousness, deceit, and blasphemy; it shall be a memorial against you for evil.

8. Woe to you, powerful ones, who by your power strike down the righteous! For the day of your destruction is coming. In those days, many **good and prosperous days** shall come to the righteous, occurring at the very time of your judgment.

# XCVII.

**Believe**, O righteous, that the sinners shall be put to shame and shall perish on the day of unrighteousness.

2. Let it be known to you that the **Most High** remembers your destruction <note>The "destruction" here refers to the end or ruin of the wicked, which God keeps in mind.</note>, and the **angels of heaven** shall rejoice over your ruin.

<summary>This page contains a series of prophetic "woes" against the wealthy and powerful who oppress the humble, concluding with a promise that the Most High and the angels will witness the eventual downfall of the wicked.</summary>
<keywords>woes, sinners, wealth, fountain of life, judgment, righteous, Most High, angels of heaven</keywords>

3. What will you do, you sinners, and where will you flee on that day of misery, when you hear the sound of the prayers of the righteous?

4. But you shall not be like them <note>Some manuscripts suggest a contrast: while the righteous pray, the sinners will be like those who provide evidence against themselves.</note>; you shall be among those who bear witness against them. This matter shall be a testimony against you: you have become companions to the sinners.

5. And in those days, the prayers of the holy ones <note>original: "qedusan". Some versions read "righteous".</note> shall reach the Lord, but for you, the days of your misery shall arrive.

6. Every word of your unrighteousness shall be read <note>original: "yitnebab", suggesting a public reading of a record of deeds.</note> before the Great Holy One; your faces shall be covered in shame, and He will cast away every deed that was founded upon unrighteousness.

7. Woe to you, sinners, who are in the middle of the sea and on the dry land; for the memory of you is evil <note>The "memory" here implies the legacy or the record of their lives held by God.</note>.

8. Woe to you who acquire silver and gold through unrighteousness and say: "We have become rich with wealth and have gained possessions; we have acquired everything we desired.

9. And now, let us do what we have planned, for we have gathered silver, and our storehouses are full like water <note>A metaphor for overflowing or abundant quantity.</note>, and many are the workers <term>harest: tenants or farm-laborers</term> in our houses."

4. ...[a slave], nor shall a **hill** become a **handmaid**; <note>The text argues that just as it is against the nature of a mountain to be a slave, sin is not a natural part of the world’s design.</note>
even so, **sin** was not sent upon the earth,
but men created it from their own heads,
and those who commit it shall come under a great curse.
5. And **barrenness** <note>original: "məknyat". Literally "cause" or "reason," but in this context often interpreted by scholars as the "cause" of lack of children (barrenness).</note> was not given to woman,
but because of the work of her own hands she dies without children.
6. I swear to you, sinners, by the **Great Holy One**,
that all your evil deeds are revealed in the heavens,
and none of your acts of **oppression** are covered or hidden.
7. And do not imagine in your spirit, nor say in your heart, that you do not know or that you do not see;
**every sin** is written down in heaven every day in the presence of the **Most High**.
8. From now on, know that all your oppression which you commit is written down every day
until the day of your **judgment**.
9. Woe to you, **fools**, for you shall perish through your ancestors!
You do not listen to the **wise**, and "good" shall not reach you.
10. And now, know that you are prepared for the day of **destruction**; and do not hope that you will live, you sinners,
but you shall go and die, because you know no **ransom**; <note>original: "beza". A term referring to the price of redemption or atonement, suggesting the sinners have no way to pay for their release from judgment.</note>
for you are prepared for the day of the great judgment, and for the day of distress and great shame for your spirits.

<header>XCVIII. 10—XCIX. 2. THE BOOK OF ENOCH</header>

...for the day of the great evil, for the day of distress and great shame for your spirit.

<margin>11.</margin>
**Woe to you, stubborn of heart**, <note>original: "gezufane lebb". Literally "thick of heart," describing those who are spiritually insensitive, obstinate, or lacking in understanding.</note> who do evil and eat **blood**! <note>In both ancient Jewish and Ethiopian Christian traditions, consuming blood was a grave sin, often associated with cruelty and pagan rituals.</note> From where do you eat good things, and drink, and are satisfied? It is from all the good things which the **Most High Lord** has multiplied upon the earth; yet you have no **peace**.

<margin>12.</margin>
**Woe to you** who love the deeds of **unrighteousness**; why do you hope for good? Know that you shall be delivered into the hands of the **righteous**; and they shall cut your necks and kill you, and they shall not show you mercy.

<margin>13.</margin>
**Woe to you** who rejoice in the distress of the righteous; for no **grave** shall be dug for you. <note>In the ancient world, being denied a proper burial was considered a terrifying fate, signifying that the person was cursed or forgotten by God.</note>

<margin>14.</margin>
**Woe to you** who make void the words of the **righteous**; for you shall have no hope of life.

<margin>15.</margin>
**Woe to you** who write **lying words** and the words of the godless; for they write down their lies so that people may hear them and lead their neighbors astray; <note>original: "labebits". The text suggests these writings cause people to forget or deceive their companions.</note> and they shall have no peace, but shall die a sudden death.

### XCIX. 
**Woe to you** who commit **impiety**, and praise **lying words**, and **deceive** <note>original: "tahsru". This refers to bringing shame upon or leading someone into error.</note> your neighbor; you shall have no good life.

<margin>2.</margin>
**Woe...**

<note>The footnotes in the original manuscript highlight several linguistic complexities:
1. The word for "spirits" varies between manuscripts, sometimes appearing as "souls."
2. The "chaotic place" refers to a hellish void outside the boundaries of the physical earth, often linked to the primordial chaos (<term>Tohu wa-Bohu</term>) mentioned in the Book of Genesis.
3. The "cloud" described in verse 4 is noted as being "not transparent" (Greek: <note>original: "οὐ διαφανές"</note>), emphasizing the murky, impenetrable nature of this place of punishment.</note>

<summary>Enoch observes a chaotic, flaming void outside the physical world where the spirits of sinners and those who perverted prophetic teachings are punished. The angel explains that this "bright" but painful place is reserved for those who defied the Lord's word.</summary>

<keywords>Judgment, Hell, Chaos, Tohu, Blasphemers, Prophets, Holy Angels, Gehenna, Vision of Enoch</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as a philological appendix, comparing various manuscript traditions of the "Book of Enoch." It specifically analyzes the lists of the "Watchers" (fallen angels) found in the Ethiopic versions and the Greek fragments (Syncellus and the Gizeh Papyrus), explaining how scribal errors and different reading methods led to discrepancies in the names and their order.</meta>

# APPENDIX ON VI. 7

The three lists of the fallen angels given above in the Ethiopic version <note>original: "**E**"</note> vi. 2, the Greek Syncellus version <note>original: "**G**^Syn"</note>, and the Greek Gizeh Papyrus <note>original: "**G**^Giz"</note>, all originate from one and the same original source. In the Ethiopic version lxix. 2 the same list reappears. In the process of copying and translating the text <note>transmission</note>, however, many corruptions and swaps in the position of words <note>transpositions</note> have occurred. In the main, the same order is observed in vi. 7; lxix. 2 and the Greek Syncellus; but a very different order is presented by the Greek Gizeh Papyrus. As the scholar Adolphe Lods <note>A prominent French biblical scholar (1867–1948) known for his work on Enoch.</note> has observed, the names in the Greek fragments were written in four columns from the third name onward. These were read from left to right by the Ethiopic and Syncellus scribes, but from top to bottom of each column by the Gizeh scribe. Within the Greek versions, certain swaps of position have occurred. These will be made clear by the following Table:

In the above Table I have followed the order of the Ethiopic version <note>original: "E"</note> chapter 69, verse 2; the names as they appear in that list head each of the twenty-one columns. Next comes the list in Ethiopic Enoch 6:7; then that in the Greek fragments of Syncellus <note>original: "G^s"</note>, and finally that in the Greek Gizeh Papyrus <note>original: "G^g"</note>. On the left of each name is placed a number which gives its place in its own list. Above each column I have put a number in brackets for convenience in references. Column (13) is placed at the end instead of after (12) since **Besesiel** <note>original: "በሰስኤል"</note> has no parallel in Ethiopic Enoch 6:7 and no certain one in the Greek Syncellus or Gizeh versions.

As regards Ethiopic Enoch 69:2, name (15) which appears again in (19) is certainly corrupt <note>meaning the scribe likely made a mistake or the text is damaged</note>, also (21) which is a repetition of (10). To (13) we have already referred. Thus the twenty-one names are reduced to nineteen.

Of Ethiopic Enoch 6:7, name (18) is missing <note>original: "wanting"</note>: also (13) is missing: (15) is hopeless <note>meaning the spelling is too garbled to identify</note>. This list furnishes nineteen names.

Of the Greek Syncellus version, name (7) is missing, and (15) and (5) are corrupt. This list has twenty names.

Of the Greek Gizeh Papyrus the list is complete, but (15) is hopeless.

In the above Table the identifications <note>confirming that two names in different lists refer to the same angel</note> may be regarded as certain in (1) (4) (6) (7-12) (14) (16) (19-20), as probable or possible in (2-3) (5) (17-18, 21), as undeterminable in (13) and (15).

# ADDITIONS AND CORRECTIONS

Page 5, column 2, line 9. For *Novationum* read *Novatianum* <note>Referring to Novatian, a 3rd-century scholar and antipope.</note>.
10, note 24. For **shall be judged** <note>original: "κριθήσονται"</note> read **shall be punished** <note>original: "κολασθήσονται"</note>, and see discussion on passage on page xxvii.
13, note 3. For ‘G⁵ omit’ read ‘G⁵ omit verse 6.’ <note>G⁵ refers to a specific Greek manuscript of Enoch.</note>
14, line 1. Emend <term>to the mountain</term> <note>original: "ለደብረ፡"</note> into <term>to a mountain</term> <note>original: "ለደብር፡"</note> with manuscript G⁵.
16, note 19. **they were eating** <note>original: "κατεσθίοσαν"</note> which I have treated as an imperfect tense is probably a unique <term>aorist</term> <note>A Greek verb form usually denoting a simple past action.</note>. In that case the reading of *a*, β-*abcux* should be followed.
17. In vii. 2 manuscript G⁵ remove the <term>obeli</term> <note>Marks used by ancient editors to indicate that a word or passage is suspected of being fake or incorrect.</note>.
19, lines 3 and 4. In manuscript G⁵ for **of them, and they transgressed and led the holy ones astray** <note>original: "αὐτῶν, καὶ παρέβησαν καὶ ἐπλάνησαν τοὺς ἁγίους"</note>⁷. 2. read **of them**⁷. 2. **and they transgressed and led the holy ones astray** <note>original: "αὐτῶν⁷. 2. καὶ παρέβησαν καὶ ἐπλάνησαν τοὺς ἁγίους,"</note>.
20, line 4 from bottom. For ‘E G⁵’ read ‘E G⁹.’
21, last line. For ‘note 12’ read ‘note 13.’
22, note 30. After *t*, β-*b* add a full stop.
26, line 5 from bottom. For ‘G⁸’ read ‘G⁹.’
33, line 11. If in **there shall not be for them mercy and peace** <note>original: "οὐκ ἔσται αὐτοῖς εἰς ἔλεον καὶ εἰρήνην"</note> the construction **into mercy** <note>original: "εἰς ἔλεον"</note> is original, then the original may have been **you shall not give them to mercy** <note>original: "לא תִּתְּנֵנוּ לרחמין"</note> = **you shall not give them to mercy** <note>original: "οὐ δώσεις αὐτοὺς εἰς ἔλεον"</note>. The construction is both Hebrew and Aramaic. Compare 1 Kings viii. 50 (Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in this place); Daniel i. 9. But most probably **there shall not be for them** <note>original: "οὐκ ἔσται αὐτοῖς"</note> is corrupt for **they themselves shall not be for mercy** <note>original: "οὐκ ἔσονται αὐτοὶ εἰς ἔλεον"</note> = **they shall not be for mercy** <note>original: "לא (יהוון) המון לרחמין"</note>. See 2 Chronicles xxx. 9.
37, note 9. For ‘note 23’ read ‘note 24.’
47, line 14. For **lightnings** <note>original: "ἀστρωπαί"</note> read **lightnings** <note>original: "ἀστραπαί"</note>.
At end of note 10 add: the manuscript reads: **receptacles** <note>original: "θήκας"</note> and **lightnings** <note>original: "ἀστραπάς"</note>.
48, last line. For **beyond** <note>original: "ἀπέκειና"</note> read **beyond** <note>original: "ἐπέκεινα"</note>.
59, note 2. For ‘xvii. 1; xxxii. 3’ read ‘xvi. 1; xxxii. 3.’
73, note 10. For ‘xviii. 1; xxii. 5, 8’ read ‘xvi. 1; xxii. 6, 9.’
83, line 10. For <term>for their praise</term> <note>original: "ለእኵቶሙ፡"</note> read <term>for their thanksgiving</term> <note>original: "ለእኵተሙ፡"</note>.
121. At end of note 2 add: <term>to the angels</term> <note>original: "ለመላእክት፡"</note> = **of angels** <note>original: "ἀγγέλων"</note> = **angels** <note>original: "מלאכים"</note>, corrupt for **kings** <note>original: "מלכים"</note>. <note>The translator suggests a scribal error where the Hebrew word for 'angels' was written instead of 'kings', which look very similar in Hebrew script.</note>
